sections.title: Immunity: innate vs adaptive
sections.highlight: INNATE = present at birth, any pathogen, same response every time. ADAPTIVE = acquired after birth, slower, SPECIFIC, has MEMORY, uses B and T cells, two types (antibody-mediated, cell-mediated).

sections.title: Innate immunity: physical barriers
sections.highlight: First line of defense: skin and mucous membranes block entry; tears, saliva, and urine wash pathogens away.

sections.title: Innate immunity: chemical mediators
sections.highlight: LYSOZYME (tears, saliva) kills bacteria. HISTAMINE, COMPLEMENT, PROSTAGLANDINS, LEUKOTRIENES promote inflammation (vasodilation + vascular permeability); some enhance phagocytosis.

sections.title: Complement
sections.highlight: Over 20 plasma proteins, normally INACTIVE. Activated by a foreign substance (bacterial wall) or by antibodies, then each activates the next (cascade). Effects: inflammation, phagocytosis, direct LYSIS of bacteria.

sections.title: Interferons
sections.highlight: Virus-infected cells release INTERFERONS, which bind NONINFECTED cells and make them produce antiviral proteins. The infected cell is not saved, but spread is limited. Some interferons activate macrophages and NK cells.

sections.title: Cells of the immune system and chemotaxis
sections.highlight: WBCs are made in red bone marrow and lymphatic tissue. CHEMOTAXIS = movement of WBCs toward chemicals released by pathogens and damaged tissue.

sections.title: Phagocytes: neutrophils and macrophages
sections.highlight: NEUTROPHILS: first to respond, die quickly, recruit other cells; pus = fluid + dead neutrophils + cells. MACROPHAGES: from MONOCYTES, enlarge in tissues, ingest more than neutrophils; monocytes + macrophages = mononuclear phagocytic system.

sections.title: Cells of inflammation: basophils, mast cells, eosinophils
sections.highlight: BASOPHILS (leave blood, enter tissue) and MAST CELLS (nonmotile, in connective tissue) release HISTAMINE and LEUKOTRIENES → inflammation; activated by complement (innate) or adaptive immunity. EOSINOPHILS REDUCE inflammation of allergies and asthma.

sections.title: Natural killer (NK) cells
sections.highlight: NK cells: a lymphocyte made in red bone marrow; recognize general classes of cells (tumor cells, virus-infected cells) and release chemicals that lyse them.

sections.title: The inflammatory response
sections.highlight: Injury/foreign substance → chemical mediators → VASODILATION (more blood flow, brings phagocytes) + phagocytes leave blood + INCREASED PERMEABILITY (fibrinogen and complement enter tissue). Fig 14.9 loop: bacteria remain → more mediators; bacteria gone → tissue repair.

sections.title: Local vs systemic inflammation
sections.highlight: LOCAL: redness, heat, swelling (blood flow + permeability), pain (swelling + mediators), loss of function. SYSTEMIC = local signs PLUS 3: marrow releases many neutrophils; PYROGENS → fever (hypothalamus); fluid loss → decreased blood volume → shock and death.

sections.title: Adaptive immunity terms: specificity, memory, antigen
sections.highlight: SPECIFICITY = recognize a particular substance. MEMORY = respond better to later exposures. ANTIGEN = substance that stimulates an immune response (foreign or self). Foreign antigens → allergy, transplant rejection. Self-antigens → autoimmune disease when they trigger destruction of healthy tissue.

sections.title: Two types of adaptive immunity
sections.highlight: ANTIBODY-MEDIATED: B cells → plasma cells → antibodies. CELL-MEDIATED: T cells (cytotoxic T destroy cells; helper T promote or inhibit BOTH types). ANTIBODY = protein made in response to an antigen.

sections.title: Origin and development of B and T cells
sections.highlight: HEMOPOIETIC STEM CELLS (red bone marrow) → all blood cells, pre-B and pre-T. B cells mature in RED BONE MARROW; T cells mature in the THYMUS. Both then move to lymphatic tissue. T cells: 4 types.

sections.title: Antigen recognition and MHC molecules
sections.highlight: Each B-/T-cell RECEPTOR binds only one specific antigen; binding activates the lymphocyte. MHC holds and PRESENTS processed antigen. CLASS I: most nucleated cells, INTERNAL antigens. CLASS II: antigen-presenting cells (macrophages, B cells, other defense cells), EXTERNAL antigens.

sections.title: Cytokines
sections.highlight: CYTOKINES = proteins secreted by a cell that regulate neighboring cells. Example: INTERLEUKIN-1 from macrophages stimulates helper T cells.

sections.title: Helper T cell activation, CD4 and CD8
sections.highlight: 6 steps: APC (macrophage) displays antigen on MHC II → helper T binds with its TCR → COSTIMULATION (interleukins + CD4) → IL-2 makes it divide → daughter helper T cells stimulate B cells and cytotoxic T cells → some become MEMORY helper T cells. CD4 on helper T (binds MHC II; bound by the AIDS virus). CD8 on cytotoxic T (MHC I).

sections.title: B lymphocyte proliferation
sections.highlight: B cell takes in the same antigen → presents it on MHC II → helper T binds (costimulation: CD4 + interleukins) → B cell divides repeatedly → some become PLASMA CELLS (make antibodies) → the rest shrink into MEMORY B CELLS.

sections.title: Antibody-mediated immunity: targets
sections.highlight: Effective against antigens in BODY FLUIDS (blood, lymph): bacteria, viruses OUTSIDE cells, toxins. Uses B cells to produce antibodies. Also involved in certain allergic reactions.

sections.title: Antibody structure
sections.highlight: Y shape. VARIABLE region = V of the Y: antigen-binding site, binds epitopes, specific. CONSTANT region = stem of the Y: same in each class, activates complement, attaches antibody to cells. Made of heavy and light chains.

sections.title: Antibody classes: IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgD
sections.highlight: IgG 80–85%: complement, phagocytosis, CROSSES PLACENTA, Rh/hemolytic disease of newborn. IgM 5–10%: complement, B-cell receptor, ABO TRANSFUSION reactions, often FIRST. IgA 15%: SALIVA, TEARS, MUCOSA, COLOSTRUM and milk. IgE 0.002%: binds MAST CELLS and BASOPHILS → inflammation. IgD 0.2%: B-cell receptor.

sections.title: Effects of antibodies
sections.highlight: DIRECT (Fig 14.14a,b): inactivate antigen; bind antigens together. INDIRECT (Fig 14.14c–e): activate complement cascade; initiate release of inflammatory chemicals (mast cells/basophils); facilitate phagocytosis (macrophages).

sections.title: Antibody production: primary vs secondary response
sections.highlight: PRIMARY: first exposure; B cell → plasma cells + memory cells; 3–14 days to make enough antibody; symptoms develop meanwhile. SECONDARY: re-exposure; MEMORY B cells quickly form plasma cells; more antibody, faster; new memory cells made.

sections.title: Cell-mediated immunity and the four T cells
sections.highlight: Against antigens IN cells and tissues: intracellular bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa. HELPER (T_H): activate macrophages, help form B cells, promote T_C. CYTOTOXIC (T_C): destroy antigen on contact. REGULATORY (T_r): turn response off when antigen is gone. MEMORY: secondary response.

sections.title: Cytotoxic T cells: activation and effects
sections.highlight: Viral antigen on MHC I → T_C's TCR binds the MHC I/antigen complex → costimulation by CD8 → helper T cells add IL-2 → T_C divides. Effects: (1) release CYTOKINES (attract macrophages → phagocytosis + inflammation; activate more T_C); (2) KILL ON CONTACT by lysis (virus-infected, tumor, transplant cells).

sections.title: Ways to acquire adaptive immunity
sections.highlight: ACTIVE = own immune system makes antibodies. Natural active: get sick (e.g., mononucleosis), can be lifelong. Artificial active: VACCINE. PASSIVE = antibodies transferred. Natural passive: mother to child (placenta, breast milk). Artificial passive: injected antibodies from a person or animal = ANTISERUM.

sections.title: Immunotherapy
sections.highlight: Treats disease by altering immune function or attacking harmful cells: boost (cytokines, agents that promote inflammation), inhibit (e.g., autoimmune disease), vaccines with monoclonal antibodies.

sections.title: Effects of aging on the lymphatic system and immunity
sections.highlight: Little effect on the lymphatic system. New T-cell production lost (thymus function lost). Primary and secondary responses decrease. Autoimmune disease and cancer increase.

sections.title: Systemic lupus erythematosus (figure only)
sections.highlight: Figure-only panel (Fig 14.19). Symptoms are highly variable: skin lesions (especially face), fever, fatigue, arthritis, anemia. Treatments: anti-inflammatory and antimalarial drugs.

sections.title: Overview and organs of the digestive system
sections.highlight: Organs, glands, and ducts transform food into nutrients. Food is broken into smaller particles; ENZYMES break them into small molecules that are ABSORBED into the blood. Fig 16.1: major digestive organs vs accessory organs (salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas).

sections.title: Five functions of the digestive system
sections.highlight: 1 INGESTION and MASTICATION, 2 PROPULSION and MIXING, 3 DIGESTION and SECRETION, 4 ABSORPTION (into blood or lymph), 5 ELIMINATION (undigested material + wastes as feces).

sections.title: The GI tract and associated organs
sections.highlight: GI tract = one long tube, mouth to anus: oral cavity, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small and large intestines, anus. Associated organs empty into it by ducts: salivary glands → oral cavity; liver with gallbladder → small intestine; pancreas → small intestine.

sections.title: Layers (tunics) of the digestive tract wall
sections.highlight: Inside → out: MUCOSA (secretes mucus; stratified epithelium in mouth/pharynx/esophagus for abrasion, columnar in stomach/intestine for secretion and absorption) → SUBMUCOSA (vessels, nerves, small glands, ANS plexus) → MUSCULARIS (longitudinal + circular; stomach adds oblique; second plexus = enteric nervous system) → SEROSA (if peritoneum) or ADVENTITIA (if not).

sections.title: Peritoneum, mesenteries, and omenta
sections.highlight: VISCERAL peritoneum (= serosa) covers organs; PARIETAL lines the abdominal wall; PERITONITIS = potentially life-threatening inflammation. MESENTERY = an organ itself, not part of the peritoneum: mesenteric domain vs nonmesenteric (formerly retroperitoneal) domain. LESSER omentum: lesser curvature → liver and diaphragm. GREATER omentum: greater curvature → transverse colon and posterior wall; omental bursa; fat.

sections.title: Oral cavity: lips, cheeks, tongue, palate, tonsils
sections.highlight: LIPS = orbicularis oris muscle covered by skin. CHEEKS contain BUCCINATOR muscles. TONGUE moves food and, with lips and cheeks, holds it during chewing. PALATE separates oral from nasal cavity: HARD (anterior, bone), SOFT (posterior, skeletal muscle + CT), UVULA extends the soft palate. Tonsils: lymphatic tissue.

sections.title: Teeth
sections.highlight: 32 adult teeth (incisors, canine, premolars, molars, wisdom), 20 primary (deciduous). Crown, neck, root. DENTIN (cellular) = bulk; ENAMEL (acellular, extremely hard) covers the crown. PULP CAVITY holds pulp (vessels, nerves, CT). Teeth sit in ALVEOLI. Caries = enamel broken down by bacterial acids; periodontal disease = inflammation of ligaments, gingiva, alveolar bone.

sections.title: Salivary glands and saliva
sections.highlight: Saliva = SEROUS (watery, enzymes: AMYLASE for carbohydrates, LYSOZYME vs bacteria) + MUCOUS (MUCIN for lubrication). PAROTID: serous, anterior to ear, duct by 2nd upper molar, MUMPS. SUBMANDIBULAR: more serous than mucous, inferior border of mandible, ducts beside the tongue frenulum. SUBLINGUAL: mostly mucous, floor of mouth. Control: mostly PARASYMPATHETIC; sympathetic → more mucous and shuts production down.

sections.title: Major digestive secretions (Fig 16.8, figure only)
sections.highlight: Figure-only table. Items that also appear in slide text are taught in their own sections. Extra items here exist only in Fig 16.8: lingual lipase, gastric lipase, cholesterol esterase, ribonuclease, deoxyribonuclease, enterokinase, sucrase, maltase, isomaltase, lactase.

sections.title: Mastication, pharynx, and esophagus
sections.highlight: Chewing increases surface area for saliva; chewed food + saliva = BOLUS. Pharynx (throat): nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx (food/drink). Esophagus: moist stratified squamous; upper ⅓ skeletal, middle ⅓ skeletal + smooth, lower ⅓ smooth; joins stomach at the CARDIAC (lower esophageal) SPHINCTER.

sections.title: Swallowing (deglutition) and peristalsis
sections.highlight: VOLUNTARY phase: bolus formed and pushed into the oropharynx. PHARYNGEAL phase: reflex starts when the bolus stimulates oropharynx receptors; EPIGLOTTIS covers the larynx. ESOPHAGEAL phase: pharynx → stomach. PERISTALSIS = wave-like contractions (wave of relaxation ahead, wave of contraction behind).

sections.title: Stomach: function, regions, and wall
sections.highlight: Storage tank, holds up to 2 L; makes mucus, HCl, protein-digesting enzymes; thick mucus layer protects from acid. Regions: CARDIAC part (gastroesophageal opening), FUNDUS (left of and superior to cardiac part), BODY (largest; greater and lesser curvature), PYLORIC part → PYLORIC SPHINCTER. Wall: 3 muscle layers (outer longitudinal, middle circular, inner oblique) for churning; RUGAE allow stretch; mucosa simple columnar with GASTRIC PITS → GASTRIC GLANDS.

sections.title: Epithelial cells of the stomach
sections.highlight: SURFACE MUCOUS cells: mucus coating (NOT in gastric glands). MUCOUS NECK cells: mucus. PARIETAL cells: HCl + INTRINSIC FACTOR. ENDOCRINE cells: hormones and paracrine molecules. CHIEF cells: PEPSINOGEN (precursor of pepsin).

sections.title: Secretions of the stomach (HCl, pepsin, mucus, intrinsic factor)
sections.highlight: Bolus + secretions = acidic CHYME. HCl: pH ≈ 2.0, kills microorganisms, activates pepsin. Acid turns PEPSINOGEN → PEPSIN, which breaks protein bonds into smaller peptide chains. MUCUS protects mucosa from acid and pepsin. INTRINSIC FACTOR binds VITAMIN B12 for absorption in the small intestine (B12: DNA synthesis, RBC production). Heartburn drugs: histamine blockers, proton pump inhibitors, antacids.

sections.title: Regulation of stomach secretion: cephalic, gastric, intestinal phases
sections.highlight: CEPHALIC: sight/smell/taste/thought → medulla → VAGUS (parasympathetic) → secretion + GASTRIN and HISTAMINE (histamine = most potent HCl stimulator). GASTRIC: food DISTENDS stomach → stretch receptors → vagal reflex + local reflexes; PEPTIDES from pepsin → GASTRIN. INTESTINAL (inhibitory): acidic chyme (pH ≤ 2) in duodenum → inhibits; local reflexes; SECRETIN (low pH) and CHOLECYSTOKININ (fatty acids, peptides) inhibit gastric secretion.

sections.title: Movement in the stomach
sections.highlight: MIXING waves: weak, mix food into chyme. PERISTALTIC waves: stronger, force chyme toward and through the pyloric sphincter. Emptying: about 4 h after a regular meal, 6–8 h after a high-fat meal.

sections.title: Small intestine: parts and lengths
sections.highlight: 6 m long; MAJOR ABSORPTIVE organ; chyme takes 3–5 h. DUODENUM: first, 25 cm, microvilli and folds, bile and pancreatic ducts. JEJUNUM: second, 2.5 m, PRIMARY site of nutrient absorption. ILEUM: third, 3.5 m.

sections.title: Small intestine mucosa: surface area and cell types
sections.highlight: Surface area: CIRCULAR FOLDS, VILLI (each with blood capillaries and a LACTEAL), MICROVILLI. Four cell types: ABSORPTIVE (microvilli, enzymes, absorb), GOBLET (mucus), GRANULAR (protect from bacteria), ENDOCRINE (hormones). Intestinal glands = CRYPTS OF LIEBERKÜHN; DUODENAL GLANDS in submucosa; PEYER'S PATCHES numerous in ileum; ILEOCECAL VALVE.

sections.title: Small intestine: secretions and movement
sections.highlight: Mucus, ions, and water protect the wall from acidic chyme and enzymes. Brush-border enzymes: PEPTIDASES (proteins → amino acids), DISACCHARIDASES (disaccharides → monosaccharides). PERISTALTIC contractions move chyme along; SEGMENTAL contractions mix over short distances. ILEOCECAL SPHINCTER mildly contracted; relaxes when peristalsis reaches it; ILEOCECAL VALVE prevents backflow into the ileum.

sections.title: Liver: anatomy, blood supply, and lobules
sections.highlight: ~3 lb, right upper quadrant under the diaphragm; RIGHT, LEFT, CAUDATE, QUADRATE lobes. PORTA = gate for vessels, ducts, nerves. HEPATIC ARTERY = O2-rich; HEPATIC PORTAL VEIN = nutrient-rich from digestive organs; out via HEPATIC VEINS → IVC. LOBULE: PORTAL TRIADS at corners (hepatic artery, portal vein, hepatic duct branches), CENTRAL VEIN in center; HEPATIC CORDS of hepatocytes; SINUSOIDS with phagocytic cells; BILE CANALICULI collect bile.

sections.title: Liver ducts and the biliary tree
sections.highlight: HEPATIC DUCTS carry bile out of the liver → left + right join as the COMMON HEPATIC DUCT → joined by the CYSTIC DUCT (gallbladder) → COMMON BILE DUCT → joins the PANCREATIC DUCT at the DUODENAL PAPILLA.

sections.title: Functions of the liver
sections.highlight: DIGESTIVE: bile neutralizes acid and emulsifies fats. EXCRETORY: bile carries cholesterol, fats, bile pigments (from hemoglobin). STORAGE: glycogen, fat, vitamins, copper, iron. CONVERSION: amino acids → lipids or glucose; fats → phospholipids; vitamin D → active. DETOX: ammonia → urea. SYNTHESIS: albumin, fibrinogen, globulins, clotting factors. 700 mL bile/day.

sections.title: Control of bile secretion and release
sections.highlight: 1 VAGUS (parasympathetic): liver secretes bile; gallbladder contracts. 2 SECRETIN (duodenum): stimulates bile secretion and release. 3 CHOLECYSTOKININ (duodenum) via blood: gallbladder contracts, sphincters relax → stored bile into duodenum. 4 BILE SALTS: positive feedback; >90% reabsorbed in the ILEUM, return via hepatic portal circulation.

sections.title: Pancreas: anatomy and secretions
sections.highlight: Posterior to the stomach, inferior part of left upper quadrant; HEAD near midline, TAIL touches spleen. ENDOCRINE: PANCREATIC ISLETS → insulin, glucagon. EXOCRINE: ACINI → digestive enzymes to the duodenum. Juice: BICARBONATE neutralizes acidic chyme; TRYPSIN, CHYMOTRYPSIN, CARBOXYPEPTIDASE (protein); PANCREATIC AMYLASE (polysaccharides); LIPASE (lipids); NUCLEASES (DNA, RNA → nucleotides).

sections.title: Regulation of pancreatic secretion
sections.highlight: 1 VAGUS → enzyme-rich secretion (sympathetic INHIBITS). 2 Acidic chyme → SECRETIN → watery secretion rich in HCO3⁻. 3 Fatty acids and amino acids → CHOLECYSTOKININ → enzyme-rich solution.

sections.title: Large intestine: anatomy and functions
sections.highlight: Absorbs water, compacts feces. CECUM (ileocecal junction; APPENDIX 9 cm lymphatic) → COLON 1.5 m (ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid; crypts make mucus; TENIAE COLI) → RECTUM → ANAL CANAL (last 2–3 cm; INTERNAL sphincter smooth/unconscious; EXTERNAL skeletal/conscious). 18–24 h transit. Microbes make VITAMIN K. MASS MOVEMENTS every 8–12 h; rectal distention → DEFECATION REFLEX.

sections.title: The digestive process: digestion, absorption, transport
sections.highlight: DIGESTION: chemical (enzymatic) vs mechanical (smaller pieces). ABSORPTION: mostly DUODENUM and JEJUNUM; some in stomach and ileum. TRANSPORT: swallowing and peristalsis. Fig 16.23: carbohydrates → monosaccharides; lipids → fatty acids + monoglycerides; proteins → amino acids.

sections.title: Carbohydrate digestion and glucose absorption
sections.highlight: Polysaccharides → disaccharides (salivary and pancreatic AMYLASES) → monosaccharides (brush-border enzymes). GLUCOSE: (1) COTRANSPORT with Na⁺ into epithelial cell; (2) driven by Na⁺ gradient from the Na⁺–K⁺ PUMP; (3) out by FACILITATED DIFFUSION; (4) into villus capillaries → HEPATIC PORTAL VEIN → liver.

sections.title: Lipid digestion, chylomicrons, and lipoproteins
sections.highlight: LIPASE: triglycerides → fatty acids + monoglycerides. BILE SALTS surround them → MICELLES. Micelles contact the cell; fatty acids and monoglycerides enter by SIMPLE DIFFUSION → re-made into triglycerides → protein coat = CHYLOMICRONS → EXOCYTOSIS → LACTEALS → lymph → blood. LIPOPROTEINS (part water-, part lipid-soluble) carry lipids in lymph and blood: chylomicrons, LDL, HDL.

sections.title: Protein digestion and amino acid absorption
sections.highlight: PEPSIN (stomach). TRYPSIN, CHYMOTRYPSIN, CARBOXYPEPTIDASE: secreted by the pancreas INACTIVE, activated in the small intestine. Brush-border PEPTIDASES on microvilli. Tri-, dipeptides, and amino acids absorbed by COTRANSPORT (many with a Na⁺ gradient); broken to amino acids inside the cell; out of the cell; into villus capillaries → HEPATIC PORTAL VEIN → liver.

sections.title: Water and minerals; fluid volumes
sections.highlight: Water moves across the intestinal wall in EITHER direction by OSMOTIC pressure; 99% of water entering the intestine is absorbed. Minerals are ACTIVELY transported across the small intestine wall. Fig 16.29: ~92% absorbed in small intestine, 6–7% in large intestine, 1% in feces.

sections.title: Effects of aging on the digestive system
sections.highlight: Connective tissue layers thin; blood supply, motility, mucus and enzyme secretions decrease; more infection, ulcers, and cancers; GERD increases.

sections.title: Diarrhea (figure only)
sections.highlight: Figure-only panel (Fig 16.30). Symptoms: increased stool frequency, volume, and fluidity. Treatments: replace lost fluid and ions; bland diet without dairy.

facts.text: Immune function can be boosted by administering cytokines or other agents that promote inflammation and activate immune cells.

facts.text: Inhibiting the immune system is used, for example, to treat an autoimmune disease.

facts.text: The slide lists vaccines with monoclonal antibodies as immunotherapy.

facts.text: Aging has little effect on the lymphatic system.

facts.cloze: With age, both {{c1::primary and secondary}} responses decrease.

facts.text: Fig 14.19 (urinary): renal lesions and glomerulonephritis can result in progressive kidney failure.

facts.cloze: The digestive system is a complex set of organs, glands, and ducts that transform food into {{c1::nutrients}} for cells.
facts.text: The digestive system is a complex set of organs, glands, and ducts that transform food into nutrients for cells.

facts.cloze: Food is broken down into smaller and smaller {{c1::particles}}.
facts.text: Food is broken down into smaller and smaller particles.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Enzymes}} break particles down into small molecules, which are absorbed into the {{c2::blood}} and transported all over the body.
facts.text: Enzymes break particles down into small molecules, which are absorbed into the blood and transported all over the body.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.1 accessory digestive organs: {{c1::salivary glands}}, {{c2::liver}}, {{c3::gallbladder}}, and {{c4::pancreas}}.
facts.text: Fig 16.1 accessory digestive organs: salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, and pancreas.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.1 labels the pharynx as the {{c1::throat}} and the oral cavity as the {{c2::mouth}}.
facts.text: Fig 16.1 labels the pharynx as the throat and the oral cavity as the mouth.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Ingestion}} is the consumption of solid or liquid food; {{c2::mastication}} is chewing.
facts.text: Ingestion is the consumption of solid or liquid food; mastication is chewing.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Propulsion}} is the movement of food from one end of the digestive tract to the other.
facts.text: Propulsion is the movement of food from one end of the digestive tract to the other.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Mixing}} is the movement of food back and forth in the digestive tract to mix it with enzymes and facilitate absorption.
facts.text: Mixing is the movement of food back and forth in the digestive tract to mix it with enzymes and facilitate absorption.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Digestion}} is the mechanical and chemical breakdown of large molecules into smaller molecules that can be absorbed.
facts.text: Digestion is the mechanical and chemical breakdown of large molecules into smaller molecules that can be absorbed.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Secretion}} is the addition of liquids, enzymes, and mucus to the ingested food.
facts.text: Secretion is the addition of liquids, enzymes, and mucus to the ingested food.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Absorption}} is the movement of molecules out of the digestive tract and into the {{c2::blood}} or {{c3::lymphatic system}}.
facts.text: Absorption is the movement of molecules out of the digestive tract and into the blood or lymphatic system.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Elimination}} is the removal of undigested material, such as fiber, plus other waste products from the body as {{c2::feces}}.
facts.text: Elimination is the removal of undigested material, such as fiber, plus other waste products from the body as feces.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.2: there is no absorption of {{c1::nutrients}} in the mouth, although some drugs can be absorbed across the oral mucosa.
facts.text: Fig 16.2: there is no absorption of nutrients in the mouth, although some drugs can be absorbed across the oral mucosa.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.2: absorption of only a few substances (e.g., water, alcohol, {{c1::aspirin}}) takes place in the stomach.
facts.text: Fig 16.2: absorption of only a few substances (e.g., water, alcohol, aspirin) takes place in the stomach.

facts.cloze: The digestive system consists of the digestive tract plus specific {{c1::associated organs}}.
facts.text: The digestive system consists of the digestive tract plus specific associated organs.

facts.cloze: The digestive tract is also called the {{c1::GI}} (gastrointestinal) tract.
facts.text: The digestive tract is also called the GI (gastrointestinal) tract.

facts.cloze: The tract is one long tube from the {{c1::mouth}} to the {{c2::anus}}.
facts.text: The tract is one long tube from the mouth to the anus.

facts.cloze: The digestive tract consists of the oral cavity, {{c1::pharynx}}, {{c2::esophagus}}, stomach, small intestines, large intestines, and anus.
facts.text: The digestive tract consists of the oral cavity, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestines, large intestines, and anus.

facts.cloze: Associated organs are not directly in the digestive tract but have {{c1::ducts}} that lead into it.
facts.text: Associated organs are not directly in the digestive tract but have ducts that lead into it.

facts.cloze: The salivary glands empty into the {{c1::oral cavity}}.
facts.text: The salivary glands empty into the oral cavity.

facts.cloze: The liver with the gallbladder empties into the {{c1::small intestine}}.
facts.text: The liver with the gallbladder empties into the small intestine.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::pancreas}} empties into the small intestine.
facts.text: The pancreas empties into the small intestine.

facts.cloze: The layers of the digestive tract wall are also termed {{c1::tunics}}.
facts.text: The layers of the digestive tract wall are also termed tunics.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::mucosa}} is the innermost layer and secretes mucus.
facts.text: The mucosa is the innermost layer and secretes mucus.

facts.cloze: In the oral cavity, pharynx, and esophagus the mucosa is {{c1::stratified}} epithelium for protection against abrasion.
facts.text: In the oral cavity, pharynx, and esophagus the mucosa is stratified epithelium for protection against abrasion.

facts.cloze: In the stomach and intestine the mucosa is {{c1::columnar}} epithelium for secretion and absorption.
facts.text: In the stomach and intestine the mucosa is columnar epithelium for secretion and absorption.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::submucosa}} contains blood vessels, nerves, small glands, and an ANS nerve plexus.
facts.text: The submucosa contains blood vessels, nerves, small glands, and an ANS nerve plexus.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::muscularis}} has longitudinal and circular muscles; the stomach adds an {{c2::oblique}} layer.
facts.text: The muscularis has longitudinal and circular muscles; the stomach adds an oblique layer.

facts.cloze: The ANS plexus of the muscularis and the plexus of the submucosa make up the {{c1::enteric nervous system}}.
facts.text: The ANS plexus of the muscularis and the plexus of the submucosa make up the enteric nervous system.

facts.cloze: The outermost layer is called {{c1::serosa}} if peritoneum is present and {{c2::adventitia}} if there is no peritoneum.
facts.text: The outermost layer is called serosa if peritoneum is present and adventitia if there is no peritoneum.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.3: the enteric nervous system consists of the {{c1::myenteric plexus}} and the {{c2::submucosal plexus}}.
facts.text: Fig 16.3: the enteric nervous system consists of the myenteric plexus and the submucosal plexus.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::visceral peritoneum}}, or serosa, is the serous membrane that covers the organs.
facts.text: The visceral peritoneum, or serosa, is the serous membrane that covers the organs.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::parietal peritoneum}} is the serous membrane that lines the wall of the abdominal cavity.
facts.text: The parietal peritoneum is the serous membrane that lines the wall of the abdominal cavity.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Peritonitis}} is potentially life-threatening inflammation of the peritoneum.
facts.text: Peritonitis is potentially life-threatening inflammation of the peritoneum.

facts.cloze: Mesenteries are double-layered, continuous sheets that hold organs in place and attach to the {{c1::posterior abdominal wall}}.
facts.text: Mesenteries are double-layered, continuous sheets that hold organs in place and attach to the posterior abdominal wall.

facts.cloze: The mesentery is an {{c1::organ}} itself, not part of the peritoneum, and has two domains.
facts.text: The mesentery is an organ itself, not part of the peritoneum, and has two domains.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::mesenteric domain}} is where all the abdominal organs are embedded and interconnect.
facts.text: The mesenteric domain is where all the abdominal organs are embedded and interconnect.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::nonmesenteric domain}} holds structures posterior to the mesenteries, formerly called {{c2::retroperitoneal}}.
facts.text: The nonmesenteric domain holds structures posterior to the mesenteries, formerly called retroperitoneal.

facts.cloze: The nonmesenteric domain includes the duodenum, {{c1::pancreas}}, ascending and descending colon, rectum, {{c2::kidneys}}, adrenal glands, and urinary bladder.
facts.text: The nonmesenteric domain includes the duodenum, pancreas, ascending and descending colon, rectum, kidneys, adrenal glands, and urinary bladder.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::lesser omentum}} connects the lesser curvature of the stomach to the liver and diaphragm.
facts.text: The lesser omentum connects the lesser curvature of the stomach to the liver and diaphragm.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::greater omentum}} connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the transverse colon and posterior body wall.
facts.text: The greater omentum connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the transverse colon and posterior body wall.

facts.cloze: The greater omentum's fold creates a cavity called the {{c1::omental bursa}} and can contain a large amount of {{c2::adipose tissue}}.
facts.text: The greater omentum's fold creates a cavity called the omental bursa and can contain a large amount of adipose tissue.

facts.cloze: The lips are muscular structures formed by the {{c1::orbicularis oris}} muscle and covered by skin.
facts.text: The lips are muscular structures formed by the orbicularis oris muscle and covered by skin.

facts.cloze: The cheeks are the lateral walls of the oral cavity; the {{c1::buccinator}} muscles flatten the cheeks against the teeth.
facts.text: The cheeks are the lateral walls of the oral cavity; the buccinator muscles flatten the cheeks against the teeth.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::tongue}} is a large muscular organ that occupies most of the oral cavity.
facts.text: The tongue is a large muscular organ that occupies most of the oral cavity.

facts.cloze: The tongue moves food and, with the lips and cheeks, holds food in place during {{c1::mastication}}.
facts.text: The tongue moves food and, with the lips and cheeks, holds food in place during mastication.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::palate}} is the roof of the oral cavity and separates it from the nasal cavity.
facts.text: The palate is the roof of the oral cavity and separates it from the nasal cavity.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::hard palate}} is the anterior part, made of bone.
facts.text: The hard palate is the anterior part, made of bone.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::soft palate}} is the posterior part, made of skeletal muscle and connective tissue.
facts.text: The soft palate is the posterior part, made of skeletal muscle and connective tissue.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::uvula}} is the posterior extension of the soft palate.
facts.text: The uvula is the posterior extension of the soft palate.

facts.cloze: Tonsils are {{c1::lymphatic tissue}} in the lateral posterior oral cavity, the nasopharynx, and the posterior surface of the tongue.
facts.text: Tonsils are lymphatic tissue in the lateral posterior oral cavity, the nasopharynx, and the posterior surface of the tongue.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.5b labels the {{c1::lingual tonsil}} and {{c2::palatine tonsil}} at the root of the tongue.
facts.text: Fig 16.5b labels the lingual tonsil and palatine tonsil at the root of the tongue.

facts.cloze: A healthy adult has {{c1::32}} teeth.
facts.text: A healthy adult has 32 teeth.

facts.cloze: There are {{c1::20}} primary (deciduous) teeth.
facts.text: There are 20 primary (deciduous) teeth.

facts.cloze: Adult tooth types: incisors, canine, premolars, molars, and {{c1::wisdom}} teeth.
facts.text: Adult tooth types: incisors, canine, premolars, molars, and wisdom teeth.

facts.cloze: Each tooth has a {{c1::crown}} with one or more cusps, a {{c2::neck}}, and a {{c3::root}}.
facts.text: Each tooth has a crown with one or more cusps, a neck, and a root.

facts.cloze: The bulk of the tooth is formed by a cellular tissue called {{c1::dentin}}.
facts.text: The bulk of the tooth is formed by a cellular tissue called dentin.

facts.cloze: In the crown, the dentin is covered by an extremely hard, acellular {{c1::enamel}}.
facts.text: In the crown, the dentin is covered by an extremely hard, acellular enamel.

facts.cloze: The center of the tooth is the {{c1::pulp cavity}}, filled with pulp: blood vessels, nerves, and connective tissue.
facts.text: The center of the tooth is the pulp cavity, filled with pulp: blood vessels, nerves, and connective tissue.

facts.cloze: Teeth are held in place within pockets in the bone called {{c1::alveoli}}.
facts.text: Teeth are held in place within pockets in the bone called alveoli.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Dental caries}} (cavities) are breakdown of enamel by acids from bacteria.
facts.text: Dental caries (cavities) are breakdown of enamel by acids from bacteria.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Periodontal disease}} is inflammation and degeneration of the periodontal ligaments, gingiva, and alveolar bone.
facts.text: Periodontal disease is inflammation and degeneration of the periodontal ligaments, gingiva, and alveolar bone.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.6 labels the {{c1::cementum}}, {{c2::root canal}}, and apical foramen in the root of a molar.
facts.text: Fig 16.6 labels the cementum, root canal, and apical foramen in the root of a molar.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.5c: teeth 1, 16, 17, and 32 are the third molars ({{c1::wisdom teeth}}).
facts.text: Fig 16.5c: teeth 1, 16, 17, and 32 are the third molars (wisdom teeth).

facts.cloze: Saliva is a mixture of {{c1::serous}} (watery) and {{c2::mucous}} fluids.
facts.text: Saliva is a mixture of serous (watery) and mucous fluids.

facts.cloze: Saliva keeps the oral cavity moist, is needed for normal {{c1::speech}}, and dissolves food particles so they can be {{c2::tasted}}.
facts.text: Saliva keeps the oral cavity moist, is needed for normal speech, and dissolves food particles so they can be tasted.

facts.cloze: Saliva protects against bacteria, neutralizes {{c1::pH}}, and begins the process of digestion.
facts.text: Saliva protects against bacteria, neutralizes pH, and begins the process of digestion.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::parotid}} glands are serous glands anterior to each ear; their duct enters the oral cavity next to the second upper molars.
facts.text: The parotid glands are serous glands anterior to each ear; their duct enters the oral cavity next to the second upper molars.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Mumps}} is inflammation of the parotid glands.
facts.text: Mumps is inflammation of the parotid glands.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::submandibular}} glands produce more serous than mucous secretions and lie along the inferior border of the mandible.
facts.text: The submandibular glands produce more serous than mucous secretions and lie along the inferior border of the mandible.

facts.cloze: The submandibular ducts open on each side of the tongue {{c1::frenulum}}.
facts.text: The submandibular ducts open on each side of the tongue frenulum.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::sublingual}} glands produce primarily mucous and lie below the mucous membrane in the floor of the oral cavity.
facts.text: The sublingual glands produce primarily mucous and lie below the mucous membrane in the floor of the oral cavity.

facts.cloze: The serous portion of saliva contains {{c1::amylase}}, which breaks down carbohydrates, and {{c2::lysozyme}}, which is active against bacteria.
facts.text: The serous portion of saliva contains amylase, which breaks down carbohydrates, and lysozyme, which is active against bacteria.

facts.cloze: The mucous portion of saliva contains {{c1::mucin}} for lubrication.
facts.text: The mucous portion of saliva contains mucin for lubrication.

facts.cloze: Saliva neutralizes pH in the mouth to protect tooth {{c1::enamel}}, which also prevents ulcerations, oral infection, and dental caries.
facts.text: Saliva neutralizes pH in the mouth to protect tooth enamel, which also prevents ulcerations, oral infection, and dental caries.

facts.cloze: Salivary amylase begins the digestion of {{c1::starch}} and polysaccharides.
facts.text: Salivary amylase begins the digestion of starch and polysaccharides.

facts.cloze: Salivary secretion is regulated by the ANS with mostly {{c1::parasympathetic}} stimulation.
facts.text: Salivary secretion is regulated by the ANS with mostly parasympathetic stimulation.

facts.cloze: Salivary secretion increases in response to tactile stimulation in the oral cavity, especially {{c1::sour}}.
facts.text: Salivary secretion increases in response to tactile stimulation in the oral cavity, especially sour.

facts.cloze: Sympathetic stimulation increases the {{c1::mucous}} content of saliva and shuts down saliva production when frightened or nervous.
facts.text: Sympathetic stimulation increases the mucous content of saliva and shuts down saliva production when frightened or nervous.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.8: {{c1::lingual lipase}} (oral cavity) and {{c2::gastric lipase}} (stomach) digest a minor amount of lipids.
facts.text: Fig 16.8: lingual lipase (oral cavity) and gastric lipase (stomach) digest a minor amount of lipids.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.8: the brush-border enzyme {{c1::enterokinase}} converts trypsinogen to trypsin.
facts.text: Fig 16.8: the brush-border enzyme enterokinase converts trypsinogen to trypsin.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.8: {{c1::lactase}} breaks apart lactose into glucose and galactose.
facts.text: Fig 16.8: lactase breaks apart lactose into glucose and galactose.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.8: {{c1::sucrase}} breaks apart sucrose into glucose and fructose.
facts.text: Fig 16.8: sucrase breaks apart sucrose into glucose and fructose.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.8: {{c1::maltase}} breaks apart maltose into two glucose molecules.
facts.text: Fig 16.8: maltase breaks apart maltose into two glucose molecules.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.8: large intestine mucus provides adhesion for {{c1::fecal matter}} and protects the wall from bacterial acids.
facts.text: Fig 16.8: large intestine mucus provides adhesion for fecal matter and protects the wall from bacterial acids.

facts.cloze: Mastication breaks food into smaller pieces, which increases the {{c1::surface area}} for interaction with saliva.
facts.text: Mastication breaks food into smaller pieces, which increases the surface area for interaction with saliva.

facts.cloze: Chewed food mixed with saliva is called a {{c1::bolus}}.
facts.text: Chewed food mixed with saliva is called a bolus.

facts.cloze: The pharynx (throat) connects the {{c1::mouth}} to the {{c2::esophagus}}.
facts.text: The pharynx (throat) connects the mouth to the esophagus.

facts.cloze: The three parts of the pharynx are the {{c1::nasopharynx}}, {{c2::oropharynx}}, and {{c3::laryngopharynx}}.
facts.text: The three parts of the pharynx are the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::oropharynx}} and {{c2::laryngopharynx}} are passageways for food and drink.
facts.text: The oropharynx and laryngopharynx are passageways for food and drink.

facts.cloze: The esophagus is a muscular tube lined with moist {{c1::stratified squamous}} epithelium that connects the pharynx to the stomach.
facts.text: The esophagus is a muscular tube lined with moist stratified squamous epithelium that connects the pharynx to the stomach.

facts.cloze: The upper third of the esophagus is {{c1::skeletal}} muscle, the middle third skeletal and smooth, and the lower third {{c2::smooth}} muscle.
facts.text: The upper third of the esophagus is skeletal muscle, the middle third skeletal and smooth, and the lower third smooth muscle.

facts.cloze: The esophagus joins the stomach at the {{c1::cardiac sphincter}} (lower esophageal sphincter).
facts.text: The esophagus joins the stomach at the cardiac sphincter (lower esophageal sphincter).

facts.cloze: Swallowing is also called {{c1::deglutition}}.
facts.text: Swallowing is also called deglutition.

facts.text: In the voluntary phase, a bolus is formed in the mouth and pushed into the oropharynx.

facts.cloze: In the {{c1::pharyngeal phase}}, the swallowing reflex is initiated when the bolus stimulates receptors in the {{c2::oropharynx}}.
facts.text: In the pharyngeal phase, the swallowing reflex is initiated when the bolus stimulates receptors in the oropharynx.

facts.cloze: During the pharyngeal phase, the {{c1::epiglottis}} covers the larynx.
facts.text: During the pharyngeal phase, the epiglottis covers the larynx.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::esophageal phase}} moves food from the pharynx to the stomach.
facts.text: The esophageal phase moves food from the pharynx to the stomach.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Peristalsis}} is wave-like contractions that move food through the digestive tract.
facts.text: Peristalsis is wave-like contractions that move food through the digestive tract.

facts.text: Fig 16.10: a wave of relaxation ahead of the mass and a wave of contraction behind it move the chyme.

facts.cloze: The stomach is a storage tank for food that can hold up to {{c1::2 liters}}.
facts.text: The stomach is a storage tank for food that can hold up to 2 liters.

facts.cloze: The stomach produces mucus, {{c1::hydrochloric acid}}, and protein-digesting enzymes.
facts.text: The stomach produces mucus, hydrochloric acid, and protein-digesting enzymes.

facts.cloze: A thick {{c1::mucus}} layer lubricates and protects the stomach's epithelial cells from acidic pH.
facts.text: A thick mucus layer lubricates and protects the stomach's epithelial cells from acidic pH.

facts.cloze: The esophagus opens into the {{c1::cardiac part}} of the stomach at the gastroesophageal opening.
facts.text: The esophagus opens into the cardiac part of the stomach at the gastroesophageal opening.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::fundus}} is to the left of, and superior to, the cardiac part.
facts.text: The fundus is to the left of, and superior to, the cardiac part.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::body}} is the largest part of the stomach.
facts.text: The body is the largest part of the stomach.

facts.cloze: The body turns to the right, creating a {{c1::greater curvature}} and a {{c2::lesser curvature}}.
facts.text: The body turns to the right, creating a greater curvature and a lesser curvature.

facts.cloze: The body narrows inferiorly to form the funnel-shaped {{c1::pyloric part}}, which ends at the {{c2::pyloric sphincter}}.
facts.text: The body narrows inferiorly to form the funnel-shaped pyloric part, which ends at the pyloric sphincter.

facts.cloze: The stomach muscularis has 3 layers: outer {{c1::longitudinal}}, middle {{c2::circular}}, and inner {{c3::oblique}}, to produce churning.
facts.text: The stomach muscularis has 3 layers: outer longitudinal, middle circular, and inner oblique, to produce churning.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Rugae}} are large folds that allow the stomach to stretch.
facts.text: Rugae are large folds that allow the stomach to stretch.

facts.text: The stomach mucosa is simple columnar epithelium with tube-like gastric pits that open into gastric glands.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Surface mucous cells}} produce mucus that coats and protects the stomach; they are not in the gastric glands.
facts.text: Surface mucous cells produce mucus that coats and protects the stomach; they are not in the gastric glands.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Mucous neck cells}} produce mucus.
facts.text: Mucous neck cells produce mucus.

facts.text: Parietal cells produce hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Endocrine cells}} produce hormones and paracrine molecules.
facts.text: Endocrine cells produce hormones and paracrine molecules.

facts.text: Chief cells produce pepsinogen, a precursor of the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.11d shows the gastric pit and gland lined, from top to bottom, by surface mucous, mucous neck, {{c1::parietal}}, {{c2::chief}}, and endocrine cells.
facts.text: Fig 16.11d shows the gastric pit and gland lined, from top to bottom, by surface mucous, mucous neck, parietal, chief, and endocrine cells.

facts.cloze: The bolus mixes with stomach secretions to form acidic {{c1::chyme}}.
facts.text: The bolus mixes with stomach secretions to form acidic chyme.

facts.text: Hydrochloric acid produces a pH of about 2.0 in the stomach.

facts.text: Hydrochloric acid kills microorganisms and activates pepsin.

facts.text: Pepsin breaks covalent bonds of proteins to form smaller peptide chains.

facts.cloze: Stomach mucus lubricates the mucosa and protects it from acidic chyme and {{c1::pepsin}}.
facts.text: Stomach mucus lubricates the mucosa and protects it from acidic chyme and pepsin.

facts.text: Intrinsic factor binds vitamin B12, making it more readily absorbed by the small intestine.

facts.text: Vitamin B12 is important in DNA synthesis and red blood cell production.

facts.text: Heartburn is a painful or burning sensation in the chest associated with increased gastric secretions and/or backflush of acidic chyme into the esophagus.

facts.text: Histamine blockers stop histamine from stimulating acid release from parietal cells.

facts.text: Proton pump inhibitors block the proton pump in parietal cells needed to make acid.

facts.text: Antacids neutralize acids in the stomach.

facts.text: In the cephalic phase, stomach secretions are initiated by sight, smell, taste, or thought of food.

facts.text: In the cephalic phase, action potentials go from the medulla oblongata along parasympathetic axons in the vagus nerves to the stomach.

facts.cloze: In the cephalic phase, neurons also stimulate release of {{c1::gastrin}} and {{c2::histamine}} from endocrine cells.
facts.text: In the cephalic phase, neurons also stimulate release of gastrin and histamine from endocrine cells.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Gastrin}} is a hormone that enters the blood and is carried back to the stomach, where it stimulates more secretion.
facts.text: Gastrin is a hormone that enters the blood and is carried back to the stomach, where it stimulates more secretion.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Histamine}} is the most potent stimulator of hydrochloric acid secretion.
facts.text: Histamine is the most potent stimulator of hydrochloric acid secretion.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::gastric phase}} is activated by the presence of food in the stomach.
facts.text: The gastric phase is activated by the presence of food in the stomach.

facts.cloze: In the gastric phase, distention stimulates {{c1::mechanoreceptors}} (stretch receptors) and activates a parasympathetic reflex.
facts.text: In the gastric phase, distention stimulates mechanoreceptors (stretch receptors) and activates a parasympathetic reflex.

facts.cloze: Distention of the stomach also activates {{c1::local reflexes}} that increase stomach secretions.
facts.text: Distention of the stomach also activates local reflexes that increase stomach secretions.

facts.cloze: In the gastric phase, {{c1::peptides}} produced by pepsin stimulate the secretion of gastrin.
facts.text: In the gastric phase, peptides produced by pepsin stimulate the secretion of gastrin.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::intestinal phase}} is controlled by the entrance of acidic chyme into the duodenum.
facts.text: The intestinal phase is controlled by the entrance of acidic chyme into the duodenum.

facts.cloze: The inhibitory influence of the intestinal phase is greatest when duodenal chyme pH drops to {{c1::2.0}} or below.
facts.text: The inhibitory influence of the intestinal phase is greatest when duodenal chyme pH drops to 2.0 or below.

facts.cloze: Duodenal chemoreceptors are stimulated by {{c1::H+}} (low pH) or {{c2::lipids}}.
facts.text: Duodenal chemoreceptors are stimulated by H+ (low pH) or lipids.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Secretin}}, released from the duodenum in response to low pH, inhibits gastric secretions.
facts.text: Secretin, released from the duodenum in response to low pH, inhibits gastric secretions.

facts.cloze: Fatty acids and peptides in the duodenum release {{c1::cholecystokinin}}, which also inhibits gastric secretions.
facts.text: Fatty acids and peptides in the duodenum release cholecystokinin, which also inhibits gastric secretions.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Mixing waves}} are weak contractions that thoroughly mix food to form chyme.
facts.text: Mixing waves are weak contractions that thoroughly mix food to form chyme.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Peristaltic waves}} are stronger contractions that force chyme toward and through the pyloric sphincter.
facts.text: Peristaltic waves are stronger contractions that force chyme toward and through the pyloric sphincter.

facts.cloze: Stomach secretions and movement are regulated by {{c1::hormonal}} and {{c2::neural}} mechanisms.
facts.text: Stomach secretions and movement are regulated by hormonal and neural mechanisms.

facts.cloze: The stomach empties about every {{c1::4}} hours after a regular meal and {{c2::6 to 8}} hours after a high-fat meal.
facts.text: The stomach empties about every 4 hours after a regular meal and 6 to 8 hours after a high-fat meal.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.13: during a peristaltic wave some chyme is forced into the duodenum, but {{c1::most chyme}} is forced back into the stomach.
facts.text: Fig 16.13: during a peristaltic wave some chyme is forced into the duodenum, but most chyme is forced back into the stomach.

facts.cloze: The small intestine measures {{c1::6 meters}} in length.
facts.text: The small intestine measures 6 meters in length.

facts.cloze: The small intestine is the major {{c1::absorptive}} organ of the gastrointestinal tract.
facts.text: The small intestine is the major absorptive organ of the gastrointestinal tract.

facts.cloze: Chyme takes {{c1::3 to 5 hours}} to pass through the small intestine.
facts.text: Chyme takes 3 to 5 hours to pass through the small intestine.

facts.cloze: The small intestine contains enzymes to further break down food and secretions that protect against the {{c1::acidity}} of chyme.
facts.text: The small intestine contains enzymes to further break down food and secretions that protect against the acidity of chyme.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::duodenum}} is the first part of the small intestine, {{c2::25 cm}} long.
facts.text: The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine, 25 cm long.

facts.cloze: The duodenum contains microvilli, many folds, and the {{c1::bile}} and {{c2::pancreatic}} ducts.
facts.text: The duodenum contains microvilli, many folds, and the bile and pancreatic ducts.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::jejunum}} is the second part, 2.5 meters long, and the primary site of nutrient absorption.
facts.text: The jejunum is the second part, 2.5 meters long, and the primary site of nutrient absorption.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::ileum}} is the third part, 3.5 meters long.
facts.text: The ileum is the third part, 3.5 meters long.

facts.cloze: The surface area of the small intestine is increased by {{c1::circular folds}} of the mucosa and submucosa.
facts.text: The surface area of the small intestine is increased by circular folds of the mucosa and submucosa.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Villi}} are tiny finger-like projections of the mucosa.
facts.text: Villi are tiny finger-like projections of the mucosa.

facts.cloze: Each villus has a loose connective tissue core containing blood capillaries and a lymphatic capillary called a {{c1::lacteal}}.
facts.text: Each villus has a loose connective tissue core containing blood capillaries and a lymphatic capillary called a lacteal.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Microvilli}} are cytoplasmic extensions of most simple columnar cells.
facts.text: Microvilli are cytoplasmic extensions of most simple columnar cells.

facts.cloze: The small intestine mucosa is simple columnar epithelium with {{c1::four}} major cell types.
facts.text: The small intestine mucosa is simple columnar epithelium with four major cell types.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Absorptive cells}} have microvilli, produce digestive enzymes, and absorb digested food.
facts.text: Absorptive cells have microvilli, produce digestive enzymes, and absorb digested food.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Goblet cells}} produce a protective mucus.
facts.text: Goblet cells produce a protective mucus.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Granular cells}} may help protect the intestinal epithelium from bacteria.
facts.text: Granular cells may help protect the intestinal epithelium from bacteria.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Endocrine cells}} produce regulatory hormones.
facts.text: Endocrine cells produce regulatory hormones.

facts.cloze: Tubular glands at the base of the villi are called intestinal glands or {{c1::crypts of Lieberkühn}}.
facts.text: Tubular glands at the base of the villi are called intestinal glands or crypts of Lieberkühn.

facts.cloze: Granular and endocrine cells are located in the {{c1::bottom}} of the intestinal glands.
facts.text: Granular and endocrine cells are located in the bottom of the intestinal glands.

facts.cloze: The submucosa of the duodenum contains mucous glands called {{c1::duodenal glands}}.
facts.text: The submucosa of the duodenum contains mucous glands called duodenal glands.

facts.cloze: Lymphatic nodules called {{c1::Peyer's patches}} are numerous in the {{c2::ileum}}.
facts.text: Lymphatic nodules called Peyer's patches are numerous in the ileum.

facts.cloze: The junction with the large intestine is the {{c1::ileocecal junction}}, containing the ileocecal valve.
facts.text: The junction with the large intestine is the ileocecal junction, containing the ileocecal valve.

facts.cloze: Secretions of {{c1::mucus, ions, and water}} lubricate and protect the intestinal wall from acidic chyme and digestive enzymes.
facts.text: Secretions of mucus, ions, and water lubricate and protect the intestinal wall from acidic chyme and digestive enzymes.

facts.cloze: Small intestine epithelial cells have enzymes bound to their {{c1::free surfaces}}.
facts.text: Small intestine epithelial cells have enzymes bound to their free surfaces.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Peptidases}} break down proteins into amino acids for absorption.
facts.text: Peptidases break down proteins into amino acids for absorption.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Disaccharidases}} break down disaccharides into monosaccharides for absorption.
facts.text: Disaccharidases break down disaccharides into monosaccharides for absorption.

facts.cloze: Mixing and {{c1::propulsion}} of chyme are the primary mechanical events in the small intestine.
facts.text: Mixing and propulsion of chyme are the primary mechanical events in the small intestine.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Peristaltic contractions}} along the length of the intestine move chyme along the small intestine.
facts.text: Peristaltic contractions along the length of the intestine move chyme along the small intestine.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Segmental contractions}} are propagated for only short distances and mix intestinal contents.
facts.text: Segmental contractions are propagated for only short distances and mix intestinal contents.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::ileocecal sphincter}} remains mildly contracted most of the time.
facts.text: The ileocecal sphincter remains mildly contracted most of the time.

facts.cloze: Peristaltic contractions reaching the ileocecal sphincter cause it to {{c1::relax}}, allowing chyme into the {{c2::cecum}}.
facts.text: Peristaltic contractions reaching the ileocecal sphincter cause it to relax, allowing chyme into the cecum.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::ileocecal valve}} prevents movement from the large intestine back into the ileum.
facts.text: The ileocecal valve prevents movement from the large intestine back into the ileum.

facts.cloze: The liver weighs about {{c1::3 lbs}} and lies in the {{c2::right upper quadrant}} under the diaphragm.
facts.text: The liver weighs about 3 lbs and lies in the right upper quadrant under the diaphragm.

facts.cloze: The liver lobes are the right, left, {{c1::caudate}}, and {{c2::quadrate}} lobes.
facts.text: The liver lobes are the right, left, caudate, and quadrate lobes.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::porta}} is the gate where blood vessels, ducts, and nerves enter and exit the liver.
facts.text: The porta is the gate where blood vessels, ducts, and nerves enter and exit the liver.

facts.cloze: The liver receives blood from the {{c1::hepatic artery}} and the {{c2::hepatic portal vein}}.
facts.text: The liver receives blood from the hepatic artery and the hepatic portal vein.

facts.cloze: The hepatic artery delivers {{c1::oxygen-rich}} blood to the liver.
facts.text: The hepatic artery delivers oxygen-rich blood to the liver.

facts.cloze: The hepatic portal vein delivers {{c1::nutrient-rich}} blood from the digestive organs.
facts.text: The hepatic portal vein delivers nutrient-rich blood from the digestive organs.

facts.cloze: Blood exits the liver through the {{c1::hepatic veins}} into the {{c2::inferior vena cava}}.
facts.text: Blood exits the liver through the hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava.

facts.cloze: Lobules have {{c1::portal triads}} at the corners and a {{c2::central vein}} in the center.
facts.text: Lobules have portal triads at the corners and a central vein in the center.

facts.cloze: Central veins collect blood leaving the lobule and unite to form the {{c1::hepatic veins}}.
facts.text: Central veins collect blood leaving the lobule and unite to form the hepatic veins.

facts.cloze: A portal triad contains branches of the hepatic artery, hepatic portal vein, and {{c1::hepatic duct}}.
facts.text: A portal triad contains branches of the hepatic artery, hepatic portal vein, and hepatic duct.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Hepatic cords}} are composed of hepatocytes and are separated by hepatic sinusoids.
facts.text: Hepatic cords are composed of hepatocytes and are separated by hepatic sinusoids.

facts.cloze: Hepatocytes take up nutrients from the portal blood to {{c1::store}}, {{c2::detoxify}}, or use them to synthesize other compounds.
facts.text: Hepatocytes take up nutrients from the portal blood to store, detoxify, or use them to synthesize other compounds.

facts.cloze: Hepatic sinusoids contain {{c1::phagocytic cells}} that remove foreign particles from blood, and also endothelial cells.
facts.text: Hepatic sinusoids contain phagocytic cells that remove foreign particles from blood, and also endothelial cells.

facts.cloze: A {{c1::bile canaliculus}} is a cleft-like lumen between cells in the cords that collects bile made by hepatocytes.
facts.text: A bile canaliculus is a cleft-like lumen between cells in the cords that collects bile made by hepatocytes.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::hepatic duct}} transports bile out of the liver.
facts.text: The hepatic duct transports bile out of the liver.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::common hepatic duct}} is formed from the left and right hepatic ducts.
facts.text: The common hepatic duct is formed from the left and right hepatic ducts.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::cystic duct}} drains the gallbladder and joins the common hepatic duct.
facts.text: The cystic duct drains the gallbladder and joins the common hepatic duct.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::common bile duct}} is formed from the common hepatic duct and the cystic duct.
facts.text: The common bile duct is formed from the common hepatic duct and the cystic duct.

facts.cloze: The common bile duct joins the {{c1::pancreatic duct}} at the {{c2::duodenal papilla}}.
facts.text: The common bile duct joins the pancreatic duct at the duodenal papilla.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.18 labels the {{c1::hepatopancreatic ampulla}} and the major and minor duodenal papillae.
facts.text: Fig 16.18 labels the hepatopancreatic ampulla and the major and minor duodenal papillae.

facts.cloze: Digestive function: bile {{c1::neutralizes stomach acid}} and {{c2::emulsifies fats}} to facilitate fat digestion.
facts.text: Digestive function: bile neutralizes stomach acid and emulsifies fats to facilitate fat digestion.

facts.cloze: Excretory function: bile contains cholesterol, fats, and {{c1::bile pigments}} that result from {{c2::hemoglobin}} breakdown.
facts.text: Excretory function: bile contains cholesterol, fats, and bile pigments that result from hemoglobin breakdown.

facts.cloze: The liver removes sugar from the blood and stores it as {{c1::glycogen}}.
facts.text: The liver removes sugar from the blood and stores it as glycogen.

facts.cloze: The liver also stores fat, vitamins, {{c1::copper}}, and {{c2::iron}}.
facts.text: The liver also stores fat, vitamins, copper, and iron.

facts.cloze: The liver converts amino acids into {{c1::lipids or glucose}}, fats into phospholipids, and vitamin D into its {{c2::active}} form.
facts.text: The liver converts amino acids into lipids or glucose, fats into phospholipids, and vitamin D into its active form.

facts.cloze: The liver removes {{c1::ammonia}} from the blood and converts it to {{c2::urea}}, which is eliminated in urine.
facts.text: The liver removes ammonia from the blood and converts it to urea, which is eliminated in urine.

facts.cloze: The liver synthesizes blood proteins such as {{c1::albumin}}, {{c2::fibrinogen}}, globulins, and clotting factors.
facts.text: The liver synthesizes blood proteins such as albumin, fibrinogen, globulins, and clotting factors.

facts.cloze: The liver secretes about {{c1::700}} milliliters of bile each day.
facts.text: The liver secretes about 700 milliliters of bile each day.

facts.cloze: Parasympathetic stimulation through the {{c1::vagus nerve}} stimulates bile secretion and causes the gallbladder to contract.
facts.text: Parasympathetic stimulation through the vagus nerve stimulates bile secretion and causes the gallbladder to contract.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Secretin}} from the duodenum also stimulates bile secretion and release.
facts.text: Secretin from the duodenum also stimulates bile secretion and release.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Cholecystokinin}}, produced by the duodenum, is carried in the blood to the gallbladder.
facts.text: Cholecystokinin, produced by the duodenum, is carried in the blood to the gallbladder.

facts.cloze: Cholecystokinin stimulates the gallbladder to {{c1::contract}} and the sphincters to {{c2::relax}}, releasing stored bile into the duodenum.
facts.text: Cholecystokinin stimulates the gallbladder to contract and the sphincters to relax, releasing stored bile into the duodenum.

facts.cloze: Bile salts increase bile secretion through a {{c1::positive-feedback}} system.
facts.text: Bile salts increase bile secretion through a positive-feedback system.

facts.cloze: Over {{c1::90%}} of bile salts are reabsorbed in the {{c2::ileum}} and carried in the blood by the hepatic portal circulation.
facts.text: Over 90% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum and carried in the blood by the hepatic portal circulation.

facts.cloze: Recycling of bile salts reduces their loss in the {{c1::feces}}.
facts.text: Recycling of bile salts reduces their loss in the feces.

facts.cloze: Bile secretion into the duodenum continues until the {{c1::duodenum empties}}.
facts.text: Bile secretion into the duodenum continues until the duodenum empties.

facts.cloze: The pancreas is located {{c1::posterior to the stomach}} in the inferior part of the left upper quadrant.
facts.text: The pancreas is located posterior to the stomach in the inferior part of the left upper quadrant.

facts.cloze: The pancreas {{c1::head}} is near the midline; the {{c2::tail}} extends to the left and touches the spleen.
facts.text: The pancreas head is near the midline; the tail extends to the left and touches the spleen.

facts.cloze: Endocrine pancreatic tissue has {{c1::pancreatic islets}}, which produce {{c2::insulin}} and {{c3::glucagon}}.
facts.text: Endocrine pancreatic tissue has pancreatic islets, which produce insulin and glucagon.

facts.cloze: Exocrine pancreatic tissues called {{c1::acini}} produce digestive enzymes that travel through ducts to the duodenum.
facts.text: Exocrine pancreatic tissues called acini produce digestive enzymes that travel through ducts to the duodenum.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Bicarbonate ions}} neutralize acidic chyme so that pancreatic and intestinal enzymes can function.
facts.text: Bicarbonate ions neutralize acidic chyme so that pancreatic and intestinal enzymes can function.

facts.cloze: The major pancreatic protein-digesting enzymes are {{c1::trypsin}}, {{c2::chymotrypsin}}, and {{c3::carboxypeptidase}}.
facts.text: The major pancreatic protein-digesting enzymes are trypsin, chymotrypsin, and carboxypeptidase.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Pancreatic amylase}} continues the polysaccharide digestion that began in the oral cavity.
facts.text: Pancreatic amylase continues the polysaccharide digestion that began in the oral cavity.

facts.cloze: The pancreatic enzyme {{c1::lipase}} is a lipid-digesting enzyme.
facts.text: The pancreatic enzyme lipase is a lipid-digesting enzyme.

facts.cloze: Pancreatic {{c1::nuclease}} enzymes degrade DNA and RNA to their component nucleotides.
facts.text: Pancreatic nuclease enzymes degrade DNA and RNA to their component nucleotides.

facts.cloze: Parasympathetic stimulation from the {{c1::vagus nerve}} causes the pancreas to release a secretion rich in digestive enzymes.
facts.text: Parasympathetic stimulation from the vagus nerve causes the pancreas to release a secretion rich in digestive enzymes.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Sympathetic}} action potentials inhibit pancreatic secretion.
facts.text: Sympathetic action potentials inhibit pancreatic secretion.

facts.cloze: Acidic chyme in the duodenum stimulates {{c1::secretin}} release.
facts.text: Acidic chyme in the duodenum stimulates secretin release.

facts.cloze: Secretin stimulates the pancreas to release a {{c1::watery}} secretion rich in {{c2::HCO3⁻}} (bicarbonate).
facts.text: Secretin stimulates the pancreas to release a watery secretion rich in HCO3⁻ (bicarbonate).

facts.cloze: Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum stimulate {{c1::cholecystokinin}} release.
facts.text: Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum stimulate cholecystokinin release.

facts.cloze: Cholecystokinin stimulates the pancreas to release an {{c1::enzyme-rich}} solution.
facts.text: Cholecystokinin stimulates the pancreas to release an enzyme-rich solution.

facts.cloze: The large intestine absorbs {{c1::water}} from indigestible food and creates compact {{c2::feces}}.
facts.text: The large intestine absorbs water from indigestible food and creates compact feces.

facts.cloze: The large intestine contains the cecum, {{c1::colon}}, {{c2::rectum}}, and anal canal.
facts.text: The large intestine contains the cecum, colon, rectum, and anal canal.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::cecum}} joins the small intestine at the ileocecal junction and has the appendix attached.
facts.text: The cecum joins the small intestine at the ileocecal junction and has the appendix attached.

facts.cloze: The appendix is a {{c1::9 cm}} lymphatic structure that is often removed.
facts.text: The appendix is a 9 cm lymphatic structure that is often removed.

facts.cloze: The colon is {{c1::1.5 meters}} long.
facts.text: The colon is 1.5 meters long.

facts.cloze: The colon contains the ascending, {{c1::transverse}}, descending, and {{c2::sigmoid}} colons.
facts.text: The colon contains the ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid colons.

facts.cloze: Longitudinal muscle of the colon forms bands called {{c1::teniae coli}}.
facts.text: Longitudinal muscle of the colon forms bands called teniae coli.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::rectum}} is a straight tube from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal.
facts.text: The rectum is a straight tube from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal.

facts.cloze: The anal canal is the last {{c1::2 to 3 cm}} of the digestive tract.
facts.text: The anal canal is the last 2 to 3 cm of the digestive tract.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::internal}} anal sphincter is smooth muscle under unconscious control; the {{c2::external}} anal sphincter is skeletal muscle under conscious control.
facts.text: The internal anal sphincter is smooth muscle under unconscious control; the external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle under conscious control.

facts.cloze: Food takes {{c1::18 to 24 hours}} to pass through the large intestine.
facts.text: Food takes 18 to 24 hours to pass through the large intestine.

facts.cloze: Feces are made of water, indigestible food, and {{c1::microbes}}.
facts.text: Feces are made of water, indigestible food, and microbes.

facts.cloze: Microbes in the large intestine synthesize {{c1::vitamin K}}.
facts.text: Microbes in the large intestine synthesize vitamin K.

facts.cloze: Feces formation is due to absorption of water and salts, secretion of {{c1::mucus}}, and action of microorganisms.
facts.text: Feces formation is due to absorption of water and salts, secretion of mucus, and action of microorganisms.

facts.cloze: Every 8 to 12 hours, strong contractions called {{c1::mass movements}} propel colon contents toward the anus.
facts.text: Every 8 to 12 hours, strong contractions called mass movements propel colon contents toward the anus.

facts.cloze: Movement of feces into the rectum distends the rectal wall and stimulates the {{c1::defecation reflex}}.
facts.text: Movement of feces into the rectum distends the rectal wall and stimulates the defecation reflex.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Chemical}} digestion is enzymatic breakdown; {{c2::mechanical}} digestion is breaking food into smaller pieces.
facts.text: Chemical digestion is enzymatic breakdown; mechanical digestion is breaking food into smaller pieces.

facts.cloze: Most absorption occurs in the {{c1::duodenum}} and {{c2::jejunum}}, although some occurs in the stomach and ileum.
facts.text: Most absorption occurs in the duodenum and jejunum, although some occurs in the stomach and ileum.

facts.cloze: Transport moves food through the digestive tract and includes {{c1::swallowing}} and {{c2::peristalsis}}.
facts.text: Transport moves food through the digestive tract and includes swallowing and peristalsis.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.23: carbohydrates are digested to {{c1::monosaccharides}}.
facts.text: Fig 16.23: carbohydrates are digested to monosaccharides.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.23: lipids are digested to {{c1::fatty acids}} and {{c2::monoglycerides}}.
facts.text: Fig 16.23: lipids are digested to fatty acids and monoglycerides.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.23: proteins are digested to {{c1::amino acids}}.
facts.text: Fig 16.23: proteins are digested to amino acids.

facts.cloze: Polysaccharides are split into disaccharides by {{c1::salivary}} and {{c2::pancreatic}} amylases.
facts.text: Polysaccharides are split into disaccharides by salivary and pancreatic amylases.

facts.cloze: Disaccharides are broken down into monosaccharides by enzymes on the surface of the {{c1::intestinal epithelium}}.
facts.text: Disaccharides are broken down into monosaccharides by enzymes on the surface of the intestinal epithelium.

facts.cloze: Glucose is absorbed into intestinal epithelial cells by {{c1::cotransport}} with {{c2::Na+}}.
facts.text: Glucose is absorbed into intestinal epithelial cells by cotransport with Na+.

facts.cloze: Glucose cotransport is driven by a sodium gradient established by a {{c1::Na+–K+ pump}}.
facts.text: Glucose cotransport is driven by a sodium gradient established by a Na+–K+ pump.

facts.cloze: Glucose moves out of the intestinal epithelial cells by {{c1::facilitated diffusion}}.
facts.text: Glucose moves out of the intestinal epithelial cells by facilitated diffusion.

facts.cloze: Glucose enters the capillaries of the intestinal villi and is carried through the {{c1::hepatic portal vein}} to the liver.
facts.text: Glucose enters the capillaries of the intestinal villi and is carried through the hepatic portal vein to the liver.

facts.cloze: Glucose enters most body cells by {{c1::facilitated diffusion}}.
facts.text: Glucose enters most body cells by facilitated diffusion.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Lipase}} breaks down triglycerides into fatty acids and {{c2::monoglycerides}}.
facts.text: Lipase breaks down triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Bile salts}} surround fatty acids and monoglycerides to form {{c2::micelles}}.
facts.text: Bile salts surround fatty acids and monoglycerides to form micelles.

facts.cloze: Micelles attach to the plasma membranes of intestinal epithelial cells, and fatty acids and monoglycerides pass in by {{c1::simple diffusion}}.
facts.text: Micelles attach to the plasma membranes of intestinal epithelial cells, and fatty acids and monoglycerides pass in by simple diffusion.

facts.cloze: Inside the intestinal epithelial cell, fatty acids and monoglycerides are converted back to {{c1::triglycerides}}.
facts.text: Inside the intestinal epithelial cell, fatty acids and monoglycerides are converted back to triglycerides.

facts.cloze: Proteins coat the triglycerides to form {{c1::chylomicrons}}, which leave the cell by {{c2::exocytosis}}.
facts.text: Proteins coat the triglycerides to form chylomicrons, which leave the cell by exocytosis.

facts.cloze: Chylomicrons enter the {{c1::lacteals}} of the villi and are carried through the {{c2::lymphatic system}} to the blood.
facts.text: Chylomicrons enter the lacteals of the villi and are carried through the lymphatic system to the blood.

facts.cloze: Lipids are packaged into {{c1::lipoproteins}} to allow transport in lymph and blood.
facts.text: Lipids are packaged into lipoproteins to allow transport in lymph and blood.

facts.cloze: Lipoproteins are part {{c1::water}} soluble and part {{c2::lipid}} soluble.
facts.text: Lipoproteins are part water soluble and part lipid soluble.

facts.cloze: Lipoproteins are needed because lymph and blood contain water and lipids are not {{c1::water soluble}}.
facts.text: Lipoproteins are needed because lymph and blood contain water and lipids are not water soluble.

facts.cloze: Lipoproteins include {{c1::chylomicrons}}, low-density lipoproteins ({{c2::LDL}}), and high-density lipoproteins ({{c3::HDL}}).
facts.text: Lipoproteins include chylomicrons, low-density lipoproteins (LDL), and high-density lipoproteins (HDL).

facts.cloze: Fig 16.27: a chylomicron is about {{c1::90%}} triglyceride.
facts.text: Fig 16.27: a chylomicron is about 90% triglyceride.

facts.cloze: Fig 16.27: LDL is the lipoprotein with the most {{c1::cholesterol}} (45%); HDL has the most {{c2::protein}} (45%).
facts.text: Fig 16.27: LDL is the lipoprotein with the most cholesterol (45%); HDL has the most protein (45%).

facts.cloze: {{c1::Pepsin}} is a protein-digesting enzyme secreted by the stomach.
facts.text: Pepsin is a protein-digesting enzyme secreted by the stomach.

facts.cloze: The pancreas secretes trypsin, chymotrypsin, and carboxypeptidase into the small intestine in an {{c1::inactive}} state.
facts.text: The pancreas secretes trypsin, chymotrypsin, and carboxypeptidase into the small intestine in an inactive state.

facts.cloze: Pancreatic protein-digesting enzymes are {{c1::activated}} in the small intestine.
facts.text: Pancreatic protein-digesting enzymes are activated in the small intestine.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Peptidases}} are bound to the microvilli of the intestinal epithelium.
facts.text: Peptidases are bound to the microvilli of the intestinal epithelium.

facts.cloze: Tripeptides, dipeptides, or individual amino acids are absorbed by various {{c1::cotransport}} mechanisms.
facts.text: Tripeptides, dipeptides, or individual amino acids are absorbed by various cotransport mechanisms.

facts.cloze: Many, but not all, amino acids are absorbed by cotransport with a {{c1::Na+}} gradient, similar to glucose.
facts.text: Many, but not all, amino acids are absorbed by cotransport with a Na+ gradient, similar to glucose.
