recall.q: Define immunity and list what it protects against.
recall.a: The ability to resist damage from foreign substances; protects against microbes, toxins, and cancer cells.

recall.q: Give four features of innate immunity.
recall.a: Present at birth; defends against any pathogen; same response every exposure; uses physical barriers, chemical mediators, cells, and inflammation.

recall.q: Give the features of adaptive immunity.
recall.a: Acquired after birth; slower than innate; specificity; memory; uses B and T cells; two types (antibody-mediated, cell-mediated).

recall.q: What are the two types of adaptive immunity?
recall.a: Antibody-mediated and cell-mediated.

recall.q: What is the first line of defense?
recall.a: Physical barriers: skin and mucous membranes.

recall.q: Which three fluids wash away pathogens and toxins?
recall.a: Tears, saliva, and urine.

recall.q: Is a physical barrier innate or adaptive?
recall.a: Innate (innate immunity is accomplished by physical barriers).

recall.q: Where is lysozyme found and what does it do?
recall.a: In tears and saliva; kills bacteria.

recall.q: Name the four chemical mediators that promote inflammation.
recall.a: Histamine, complement, prostaglandins, leukotrienes.

recall.q: How do those mediators promote inflammation?
recall.a: By causing vasodilation and increasing vascular permeability; some also enhance phagocytosis.

recall.q: What is complement?
recall.a: A group of over 20 proteins in blood plasma, normally inactive.

recall.q: What activates complement?
recall.a: Combining with a foreign substance (e.g., parts of a bacterial wall) or with antibodies.

recall.q: List the three effects of activated complement.
recall.a: Promotes inflammation, promotes phagocytosis, directly lyses bacterial cells.

recall.q: What do interferons protect against?
recall.a: Viral infections.

recall.q: Which cells do interferons act on, and what do those cells make?
recall.a: Noninfected cells; they produce antiviral proteins.

recall.q: Do interferons save the cell that made them?
recall.a: No. The infected cell cannot be protected; interferons keep the virus from spreading.

recall.q: Where are white blood cells produced?
recall.a: Red bone marrow and lymphatic tissues.

recall.q: Define chemotaxis.
recall.a: Movement of WBCs toward chemicals released by pathogens and damaged tissues.

recall.q: What do WBCs do after being attracted?
recall.a: Leave the blood and enter the affected tissues.

recall.q: Name the two most important phagocytes.
recall.a: Neutrophils and macrophages.

recall.q: Describe neutrophils (3 points).
recall.a: First to respond to infection; die quickly; release chemicals that recruit and activate other immune cells.

recall.q: What is pus?
recall.a: An accumulation of fluid, dead neutrophils, and other cells at an infection site.

recall.q: Where do macrophages come from and how do they compare with neutrophils?
recall.a: From monocytes that leave the blood, enter tissues, and enlarge; they can ingest more than neutrophils.

recall.q: Which two cells release histamine and leukotrienes?
recall.a: Basophils and mast cells.

recall.q: How do basophils and mast cells differ in location/motility?
recall.a: Basophils leave the blood and enter infected tissues; mast cells are nonmotile cells in connective tissue.

recall.q: What do eosinophils do?
recall.a: Release chemicals that reduce inflammation associated with allergies and asthma.

recall.q: What type of cell is an NK cell and where is it produced?
recall.a: A lymphocyte, produced in red bone marrow.

recall.q: Which cells do NK cells recognize?
recall.a: General classes of cells such as tumor cells or virus-infected cells.

recall.q: How do NK cells kill?
recall.a: They release chemicals which lyse cells.

recall.q: What signals the inflammatory response?
recall.a: The presence of a foreign substance (chemicals and cells produced due to injury).

recall.q: List the three effects of the chemical mediators in inflammation.
recall.a: Vasodilation (more blood flow, brings phagocytes/WBCs); phagocytes leave the blood and enter tissue; increased vascular permeability lets fibrinogen and complement in.

recall.q: In Fig 14.9, what happens if bacteria remain?
recall.a: Additional chemical mediators are activated and the cycle repeats.

recall.q: List the symptoms of local inflammation and their causes.
recall.a: Redness, heat, swelling (blood flow and permeability); pain (swelling and mediators); loss of function (tissue destruction, swelling, pain).

recall.q: Name the three extra features of systemic inflammation.
recall.a: Large numbers of neutrophils released from marrow; pyrogens cause fever; fluid loss can cause shock and death.

recall.q: How do pyrogens cause fever?
recall.a: They affect the temperature-regulating mechanism in the hypothalamus.

recall.q: Define specificity and memory.
recall.a: Specificity: ability to recognize a particular substance. Memory: ability to respond with increasing effectiveness to successive exposures.

recall.q: Define antigen and give examples.
recall.a: A substance that stimulates an immune response; bacteria, virus, pollen, food, drugs.

recall.q: What two problems can foreign antigens cause?
recall.a: Allergic reactions (overreaction) and rejection of tissue and organ transplants.

recall.q: What is an autoimmune disease?
recall.a: When self-antigens stimulate unwanted destruction of healthy tissue.

recall.q: Which cells make antibodies, and from which cells do they come?
recall.a: Plasma cells, which come from B cells.

recall.q: Name the two T cells listed under cell-mediated immunity and their roles.
recall.a: Cytotoxic T cells destroy cells; helper T cells promote or inhibit both antibody-mediated and cell-mediated immunity.

recall.q: Define antibody.
recall.a: A protein the body produces in response to an antigen.

recall.q: Where do hemopoietic stem cells live and what do they give rise to?
recall.a: Red bone marrow; all blood cells, including pre-B and pre-T cells.

recall.q: Where do B cells mature? Where do T cells mature?
recall.a: B cells in red bone marrow; T cells in the thymus gland.

recall.q: Where do both go after maturing?
recall.a: To lymphatic tissue.

recall.q: Which type of immunity do T cells mainly serve?
recall.a: Cell-mediated, but they also participate in antibody-mediated immunity.

recall.q: What happens when a lymphocyte's antigen receptor combines with its antigen?
recall.a: The lymphocyte is activated and adaptive immunity begins.

recall.q: What does an MHC molecule do?
recall.a: Contains binding sites for antigens, holds and presents a processed antigen on the cell surface, and binds the antigen receptor on B or T cells to stimulate a response.

recall.q: Compare MHC class I and class II.
recall.a: Class I: most nucleated cells, internal antigens. Class II: antigen-presenting cells, external antigens.

recall.q: Name two antigen-presenting cells.
recall.a: Macrophages and B cells (and other defense cells).

recall.q: Define cytokine.
recall.a: A protein secreted by a cell that regulates neighboring cells.

recall.q: Give the slide's example of a cytokine.
recall.a: Interleukin-1 released by macrophages stimulates helper T cells.

recall.q: Which cytokine from helper T cells activates cytotoxic T cells?
recall.a: Interleukin-2.

recall.q: List the 6 steps of helper T cell activation.
recall.a: APC displays antigen on MHC II; helper T binds via TCR; costimulation (interleukins, CD4); IL-2 activates division; daughter cells stimulate B and cytotoxic T cells; some become memory T cells.

recall.q: Which surface molecule is on helper T cells and what does it bind?
recall.a: CD4; binds MHC class II molecules.

recall.q: Which surface molecule is on cytotoxic T cells and what does it bind?
recall.a: CD8; connects to cells displaying MHC class I.

recall.q: Which cells does the AIDS virus infect, and through which molecule?
recall.a: Helper T cells, through CD4.

recall.q: How is the antigen presented by a B cell?
recall.a: Processed and presented on the B-cell surface by an MHC class II molecule.

recall.q: What two cell types come from the dividing B cells?
recall.a: Plasma cells (produce antibodies) and memory B cells.

recall.q: What is the role of the helper T cell in B-cell proliferation?
recall.a: It binds the MHC II/antigen complex on the B cell, with costimulation by CD4 and interleukins, which causes the B cell to divide.

recall.q: Where are the antigens that antibody-mediated immunity acts against?
recall.a: In body fluids (blood and lymph).

recall.q: What targets does antibody-mediated immunity work against?
recall.a: Bacteria, viruses outside cells, toxins.

recall.q: Compare its targets with cell-mediated immunity.
recall.a: Antibody-mediated: antigens in body fluids. Cell-mediated: antigens in cells and tissues (intracellular bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa).

recall.q: Describe the variable region.
recall.a: The V of the Y; binds epitopes of antigen with the antigen-binding site; binds only a specific antigen.

recall.q: Describe the constant region.
recall.a: The stem of the Y; same structure within each immunoglobulin class; can activate complement and attach the antibody to a cell.

recall.q: Which two chain types make up an antibody?
recall.a: Heavy chains and light chains.

recall.q: Which antibody crosses the placenta, and which disease of the newborn is it responsible for?
recall.a: IgG; Rh reactions such as hemolytic disease of the newborn.

recall.q: Give four facts about IgM.
recall.a: 5–10% of serum antibody; activates complement; antigen receptor on B cells; ABO transfusion reactions; often the first antibody produced.

recall.q: Where is IgA found?
recall.a: Saliva, tears, mucous membranes, colostrum and milk.

recall.q: What does IgE bind to and what does it cause?
recall.a: Mast cells and basophils; stimulates the inflammatory response.

recall.q: Which two antibodies act as antigen-binding receptors on B cells?
recall.a: IgM and IgD.

recall.q: List the five effects of antibodies.
recall.a: Inactivate antigen; bind antigens together; activate complement cascades; initiate release of inflammatory chemicals; facilitate phagocytosis.

recall.q: Which two effects are direct (Fig 14.14a,b)?
recall.a: Inactivating the antigen and binding several antigens together.

recall.q: Which cells carry out the indirect effects in Fig 14.14d and e?
recall.a: Mast cells or basophils (inflammatory chemicals) and macrophages (phagocytosis).

recall.q: Describe the primary response.
recall.a: First exposure; B cell divides into plasma cells and memory cells; 3–14 days to make enough antibody; symptoms develop meanwhile.

recall.q: Describe the secondary response.
recall.a: Re-exposure to a known antigen; memory B cells quickly divide into plasma cells that produce antibodies; new memory cells form.

recall.q: Compare the two responses in Fig 14.15.
recall.a: Primary: fewer plasma cells and antibodies, longer response time (3–14 days). Secondary: more plasma cells and antibodies, shorter response time (hours to a few days).

recall.q: What does cell-mediated immunity act against?
recall.a: Antigens in cells and tissues: intracellular bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa.

recall.q: Name the four T cells of cell-mediated immunity.
recall.a: Helper, cytotoxic, regulatory, memory.

recall.q: What do regulatory T cells do?
recall.a: Turn off the immune response when the antigen is gone.

recall.q: How do cytotoxic T cells recognize virus-infected cells?
recall.a: Their T-cell receptor binds the MHC class I/viral antigen complex, which is not present on uninfected cells.

recall.q: Name the two costimulation sources for cytotoxic T cells.
recall.a: Surface molecules such as CD8, and cytokines such as interleukin-2 from helper T cells.

recall.q: List the two main effects of cytotoxic T cells.
recall.a: Release cytokines (attract macrophages, activate more cytotoxic T cells); contact and kill target cells by lysis.

recall.q: Which three kinds of cells stimulate cytotoxic T-cell killing?
recall.a: Virally infected cells, tumor cells, and tissue transplants.

recall.q: Give the four ways to acquire adaptive immunity with one example each.
recall.a: Natural active (illness, e.g., mononucleosis); natural passive (placenta, breast milk); artificial active (vaccine); artificial passive (antiserum).

recall.q: What is the difference between active and passive immunity?
recall.a: Active: immunity provided by the person's own immune system. Passive: immunity transferred from another person or animal.

recall.q: What is antiserum?
recall.a: Injected antibodies from another person or animal (artificially acquired passive immunity).

recall.q: Define immunotherapy.
recall.a: Treating disease by altering immune system function or directly attacking harmful cells.

recall.q: How can immune function be boosted?
recall.a: By administering cytokines or other agents that promote inflammation and activate immune cells.

recall.q: When is the immune system inhibited?
recall.a: For example, in treating an autoimmune disease.

recall.q: Why is new T-cell production lost with age?
recall.a: Because of loss of thymus function.

recall.q: What happens to primary and secondary responses with age?
recall.a: Both decrease.

recall.q: Which two conditions increase with age?
recall.a: Autoimmune diseases and cancer.

recall.q: List SLE's general symptoms from Fig 14.19.
recall.a: Skin lesions (particularly on face), fever, fatigue, arthritis, anemia.

recall.q: Which two drug groups treat SLE in Fig 14.19?
recall.a: Anti-inflammatory drugs and antimalarial drugs.

recall.q: What kidney problem does Fig 14.19 list for SLE?
recall.a: Renal lesions and glomerulonephritis, which can lead to progressive kidney failure.

recall.q: What does the digestive system do, in one sentence?
recall.a: A set of organs, glands, and ducts that transforms food into nutrients for cells.

recall.q: What breaks food particles into small molecules, and where do those molecules go?
recall.a: Enzymes; the small molecules are absorbed into the blood and transported all over the body.

recall.q: Name the accessory digestive organs in Fig 16.1.
recall.a: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas.

recall.q: List the five functions of the digestive system.
recall.a: Ingestion and mastication; propulsion and mixing; digestion and secretion; absorption; elimination.

recall.q: Distinguish propulsion from mixing.
recall.a: Propulsion moves food from one end of the tract to the other; mixing moves it back and forth to mix it with enzymes and facilitate absorption.

recall.q: Define absorption.
recall.a: Movement of molecules out of the digestive tract into the blood or lymphatic system.

recall.q: What is eliminated as feces?
recall.a: Undigested material such as fiber, plus other waste products.

recall.q: List the parts of the digestive tract in order.
recall.a: Oral cavity, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestines, large intestines, anus.

recall.q: How do associated organs connect to the tract?
recall.a: Through ducts that lead into the tract.

recall.q: Where does each associated organ empty?
recall.a: Salivary glands → oral cavity; liver with gallbladder → small intestine; pancreas → small intestine.

recall.q: Name the four tunics from innermost to outermost.
recall.a: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, serosa/adventitia.

recall.q: Why does the mucosa differ between the esophagus and the stomach?
recall.a: Esophagus: stratified epithelium for protection against abrasion. Stomach: columnar epithelium for secretion and absorption.

recall.q: What makes up the enteric nervous system?
recall.a: The ANS plexus of the muscularis together with the plexus of the submucosa.

recall.q: Serosa vs adventitia?
recall.a: Outermost layer is serosa if peritoneum is present, adventitia if not.

recall.q: Distinguish visceral from parietal peritoneum.
recall.a: Visceral (serosa) covers the organs; parietal lines the wall of the abdominal cavity.

recall.q: What is peritonitis?
recall.a: Potentially life-threatening inflammation of the peritoneum.

recall.q: What are the two domains of the mesentery?
recall.a: Mesenteric domain (abdominal organs embedded and interconnected) and nonmesenteric domain (posterior structures, formerly retroperitoneal).

recall.q: Compare the lesser and greater omentum.
recall.a: Lesser: lesser curvature of stomach to liver and diaphragm. Greater: greater curvature to transverse colon and posterior body wall; forms the omental bursa; can hold much fat.

recall.q: Which muscle forms the lips and which is in the cheeks?
recall.a: Orbicularis oris (lips); buccinator (cheeks).

recall.q: Compare the hard and soft palate.
recall.a: Hard palate: anterior, bone. Soft palate: posterior, skeletal muscle and connective tissue; the uvula extends from it.

recall.q: Where are the tonsils located according to the digestive deck?
recall.a: Lateral posterior oral cavity, nasopharynx, and posterior surface of the tongue.

recall.q: How many adult and primary teeth are there?
recall.a: 32 adult; 20 primary (deciduous).

recall.q: Compare dentin and enamel.
recall.a: Dentin: cellular, forms the bulk of the tooth. Enamel: extremely hard, acellular, covers the dentin of the crown.

recall.q: What fills the pulp cavity?
recall.a: Pulp: blood vessels, nerves, and connective tissue.

recall.q: Define dental caries and periodontal disease.
recall.a: Caries: breakdown of enamel by acids from bacteria. Periodontal disease: inflammation and degeneration of periodontal ligaments, gingiva, and alveolar bone.

recall.q: Name the three salivary glands and their main secretion.
recall.a: Parotid: serous. Submandibular: more serous than mucous. Sublingual: primarily mucous.

recall.q: Which enzymes are in the serous portion of saliva and what do they do?
recall.a: Amylase (breaks down carbohydrates) and lysozyme (active against bacteria).

recall.q: List three protective functions of saliva.
recall.a: Prevents bacterial infection with lysozyme; neutralizes pH to protect enamel; neutralizing also prevents ulcerations, oral infection, and caries.

recall.q: How does the ANS control salivation?
recall.a: Mostly parasympathetic stimulation; sympathetic stimulation increases mucous content and shuts production down when frightened or nervous.

recall.q: Which brush-border enzyme in Fig 16.8 activates trypsinogen?
recall.a: Enterokinase.

recall.q: Name the four disaccharide-splitting enzymes in Fig 16.8.
recall.a: Sucrase, maltase, isomaltase, lactase.

recall.q: Which minor lipid-digesting enzymes come from the oral cavity and stomach in Fig 16.8?
recall.a: Lingual lipase and gastric lipase.

recall.q: What is a bolus?
recall.a: Chewed food mixed with saliva.

recall.q: Name the three parts of the pharynx; which carry food?
recall.a: Nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx; the oropharynx and laryngopharynx are passageways for food/drink.

recall.q: Describe the muscle of the esophagus by thirds.
recall.a: Upper third skeletal; middle third skeletal and smooth; lower third smooth.

recall.q: Where does the esophagus join the stomach?
recall.a: At the cardiac (lower esophageal) sphincter.

recall.q: Name the three phases of swallowing in order.
recall.a: Voluntary, pharyngeal, esophageal.

recall.q: What starts the swallowing reflex?
recall.a: The bolus stimulating receptors in the oropharynx.

recall.q: What prevents food from entering the larynx?
recall.a: The epiglottis covers the larynx during the pharyngeal phase.

recall.q: List the regions of the stomach from esophagus to duodenum.
recall.a: Cardiac part, fundus, body, pyloric part ending at the pyloric sphincter.

recall.q: Name the three muscle layers of the stomach and their purpose.
recall.a: Outer longitudinal, middle circular, inner oblique; produce churning action.

recall.q: What are rugae?
recall.a: Large folds that allow the stomach to stretch.

recall.q: What protects the stomach wall from its own acid?
recall.a: A thick mucus layer that lubricates and protects the epithelial cells.

recall.q: Which stomach cell makes HCl, and what else does it make?
recall.a: Parietal cells; also intrinsic factor.

recall.q: Which cell makes pepsinogen?
recall.a: Chief cells.

recall.q: Which mucus-producing cell is NOT in the gastric glands?
recall.a: Surface mucous cells.

recall.q: What are the two functions of HCl in the stomach?
recall.a: Kills microorganisms and activates pepsin (pH about 2.0).

recall.q: How is pepsin formed and what does it do?
recall.a: Acid activates pepsinogen to pepsin; pepsin breaks covalent bonds of proteins into smaller peptide chains.

recall.q: What does intrinsic factor do, and why does it matter?
recall.a: Binds vitamin B12 so the small intestine absorbs it; B12 is needed for DNA synthesis and RBC production.

recall.q: Name the three heartburn medications and how each works.
recall.a: Histamine blockers (stop histamine stimulating acid release), proton pump inhibitors (block the parietal-cell proton pump), antacids (neutralize stomach acid).

recall.q: Name the three phases of gastric regulation and what starts each.
recall.a: Cephalic: sight, smell, taste, thought of food. Gastric: food in the stomach (distention, peptides). Intestinal: acidic chyme entering the duodenum.

recall.q: Which nerve carries the cephalic and gastric phase signals?
recall.a: The vagus nerves (parasympathetic).

recall.q: Which substance is the most potent stimulator of HCl secretion?
recall.a: Histamine.

recall.q: Which two duodenal hormones inhibit gastric secretion, and what releases each?
recall.a: Secretin (low pH) and cholecystokinin (fatty acids and peptides).

recall.q: Compare mixing and peristaltic waves in the stomach.
recall.a: Mixing waves: weak, mix food into chyme. Peristaltic waves: stronger, force chyme toward and through the pyloric sphincter.

recall.q: How long does the stomach take to empty after a regular meal vs a fatty meal?
recall.a: About 4 hours vs 6 to 8 hours.

recall.q: What happens to most chyme during a peristaltic wave (Fig 16.13)?
recall.a: Most is forced back into the stomach; some is forced into the duodenum.

recall.q: Name the three parts of the small intestine with their lengths.
recall.a: Duodenum 25 cm; jejunum 2.5 m; ileum 3.5 m.

recall.q: Which part is the primary site of nutrient absorption?
recall.a: The jejunum.

recall.q: Which part receives the bile and pancreatic ducts?
recall.a: The duodenum.

recall.q: How long does chyme take to pass through the small intestine?
recall.a: 3 to 5 hours.

recall.q: Name three modifications that increase the small intestine's surface area.
recall.a: Circular folds, villi, microvilli.

recall.q: What does the core of a villus contain?
recall.a: Loose connective tissue with blood capillaries and a lacteal (lymphatic capillary).

recall.q: List the four cell types of the small intestine mucosa and their roles.
recall.a: Absorptive (microvilli, enzymes, absorb food); goblet (mucus); granular (protect from bacteria); endocrine (hormones).

recall.q: Where are Peyer's patches numerous?
recall.a: In the ileum.

recall.q: Which brush-border enzymes are named on D63 and what do they do?
recall.a: Peptidases (proteins → amino acids) and disaccharidases (disaccharides → monosaccharides).

recall.q: Compare peristaltic and segmental contractions.
recall.a: Peristaltic: along the length, move chyme along. Segmental: short distances, mix contents.

recall.q: What lets chyme into the cecum, and what stops it from coming back?
recall.a: Peristalsis reaching the ileocecal sphincter makes it relax; the ileocecal valve prevents backflow into the ileum.

recall.q: Name the four lobes of the liver.
recall.a: Right, left, caudate, quadrate.

recall.q: Compare the two blood supplies of the liver.
recall.a: Hepatic artery: oxygen-rich blood. Hepatic portal vein: nutrient-rich blood from the digestive organs.

recall.q: What is in a portal triad?
recall.a: Branches of the hepatic artery, hepatic portal vein, and hepatic duct.

recall.q: Trace blood out of a lobule.
recall.a: Sinusoids → central vein → hepatic veins → inferior vena cava.

recall.q: Which two ducts form the common bile duct?
recall.a: The common hepatic duct and the cystic duct.

recall.q: Where does the common bile duct end?
recall.a: It joins the pancreatic duct at the duodenal papilla.

recall.q: Trace bile from the liver to the duodenum.
recall.a: Hepatic ducts → common hepatic duct → (joined by cystic duct) common bile duct → joins pancreatic duct at duodenal papilla → duodenum.

recall.q: List the six groups of liver functions.
recall.a: Digestive, excretory, nutrient storage, nutrient conversion, detoxification, synthesis of new molecules.

recall.q: What does the liver do with ammonia?
recall.a: Removes it from the blood and converts it to urea, eliminated in urine.

recall.q: Name the blood proteins the liver synthesizes.
recall.a: Albumin, fibrinogen, globulins, clotting factors.

recall.q: How much bile does the liver secrete per day?
Name the three signals that stimulate bile secretion or release.
recall.a: Vagus nerve (parasympathetic), secretin, cholecystokinin.

recall.q: What does cholecystokinin do to the gallbladder?
recall.a: Stimulates it to contract and the sphincters to relax, releasing stored bile into the duodenum.

recall.q: Describe the bile salt feedback loop.
recall.a: Over 90% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum, return to the liver via the hepatic portal circulation, and stimulate further bile secretion (positive feedback).

recall.q: Distinguish the endocrine and exocrine pancreas.
recall.a: Endocrine: pancreatic islets make insulin and glucagon. Exocrine: acini make digestive enzymes sent through ducts to the duodenum.

recall.q: Why is bicarbonate needed?
recall.a: It neutralizes acidic chyme so pancreatic and intestinal enzymes can function.

recall.q: Name the three pancreatic protein-digesting enzymes.
recall.a: Trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase.

recall.q: Name the pancreatic enzymes for carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids.
recall.a: Pancreatic amylase, lipase, nucleases.

recall.q: Which stimulus causes a bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion, and through which hormone?
recall.a: Acidic chyme in the duodenum, through secretin.

recall.q: Which stimulus causes an enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion, and through which hormone?
recall.a: Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum, through cholecystokinin (also the vagus nerve).

recall.q: What does sympathetic stimulation do to pancreatic secretion?
recall.a: Inhibits it.

recall.q: List the parts of the large intestine in order.
recall.a: Cecum, colon (ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid), rectum, anal canal.

recall.q: Compare the internal and external anal sphincters.
recall.a: Internal: smooth muscle, unconscious control. External: skeletal muscle, conscious control.

recall.q: What are mass movements?
recall.a: Strong contractions every 8 to 12 hours that propel colon contents toward the anus.

recall.q: What do large-intestine microbes synthesize?
recall.a: Vitamin K.

recall.q: Distinguish chemical from mechanical digestion.
recall.a: Chemical: enzymatic breakdown. Mechanical: breaking food into smaller pieces.

recall.q: Where does most absorption occur?
recall.a: Duodenum and jejunum (some in stomach and ileum).

recall.q: What are the end products of carbohydrate, lipid, and protein digestion (Fig 16.23)?
recall.a: Monosaccharides; fatty acids and monoglycerides; amino acids.

recall.q: Which enzymes split polysaccharides, and which split disaccharides?
recall.a: Salivary and pancreatic amylases split polysaccharides; brush-border enzymes on the intestinal epithelium split disaccharides.

recall.q: List the four steps of glucose absorption.
recall.a: Cotransport with Na+ into the cell; Na+ gradient made by the Na+–K+ pump; facilitated diffusion out; into villus capillaries and hepatic portal vein to the liver.

recall.q: Where does absorbed glucose go first?
recall.a: Through the hepatic portal vein to the liver.

recall.q: What does lipase produce from triglycerides?
recall.a: Fatty acids and monoglycerides.

recall.q: What is a micelle and how does it help absorption?
recall.a: Bile salts surrounding fatty acids and monoglycerides; it attaches to the epithelial cell so they pass in by simple diffusion.

recall.q: Trace a fat from inside the epithelial cell to the blood.
recall.a: Fatty acids + monoglycerides → triglycerides → protein coat = chylomicron → exocytosis → lacteal → lymphatic system → blood.

recall.q: Why are lipoproteins needed, and name three.
recall.a: Lipids are not water soluble but lymph and blood are watery; chylomicrons, LDL, HDL.

recall.q: Which protein-digesting enzymes come from the stomach and from the pancreas?
recall.a: Stomach: pepsin. Pancreas: trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase.

recall.q: In what state are pancreatic proteases secreted, and where are they activated?
recall.a: Inactive; activated in the small intestine.

recall.q: Trace an absorbed amino acid to the liver.
recall.a: Cotransport (often with Na+) into the epithelial cell → out of the cell → villus blood capillaries → hepatic portal vein → liver.

recall.q: What determines the direction of water movement across the intestinal wall?
recall.a: Osmotic pressures.

recall.q: What percentage of water entering the intestine is absorbed?
How are minerals absorbed?
recall.a: Actively transported across the small intestine wall.

recall.q: List four things that decrease in the aging GI tract.
recall.a: Thickness of connective tissue layers, blood supply, motility, mucus and digestive enzyme secretions.

recall.q: What increases with aging in the GI tract?
recall.a: Susceptibility to infection, ulcers, and cancers; GERD.

recall.q: What happens to motility with age?
recall.a: It decreases.

recall.q: List the three symptoms of diarrhea in Fig 16.30.
recall.a: Increased stool frequency, volume, and fluidity.

recall.q: What are the treatments in Fig 16.30?
recall.a: Replacing lost fluid and ions; eating a bland diet without dairy.

recall.q: Which acid–base problem does the urinary box of Fig 16.30 name?
recall.a: Metabolic acidosis (the kidney compensates).

quiz.stem: Which feature belongs to adaptive immunity but NOT to innate immunity?
options: Memory that gives a faster response on later exposures
Same response every time the body is exposed
quiz.explanation: L26: adaptive immunity has memory; L25: innate immunity is present at birth, gives the same response each time, and defends against any pathogen.

quiz.stem: All of the following accomplish innate immunity, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: L25 lists physical barriers, chemical mediators, cells, and inflammatory response. Antibody production by plasma cells is adaptive (L44).

quiz.stem: A child meets a bacterium for the first time. Compared with the innate response, the adaptive response to it will be:
options: Slower, but specific to that bacterium
quiz.explanation: L26: adaptive immunity is slower than innate immunity and has specificity (recognizes a particular substance).

quiz.stem: Innate immunity is also called:
quiz.explanation: L24: innate (nonspecific resistance); adaptive (specific immunity).

quiz.stem: Which fluids are listed as washing away pathogens and toxins?
quiz.explanation: L28: 'Tears, saliva, urine wash away pathogens and toxins.'

quiz.stem: A burn destroys a large area of skin. Which part of innate immunity is lost over that area?
options: A physical barrier, the first line of defense
quiz.explanation: L28: skin and mucous membranes act as barriers to pathogens and toxins; physical barriers are the first line of defense.

quiz.stem: Which chemical mediator, found in tears and saliva, kills bacteria?
quiz.explanation: L29: Lysozyme, found in tears and saliva to kill bacteria.

quiz.stem: Histamine, complement, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes promote inflammation mainly by:
options: Presenting antigen on MHC class I
Causing vasodilation and increasing vascular permeability
quiz.explanation: L30: they promote inflammation by causing vasodilation and increasing vascular permeability.

quiz.stem: All of the following are listed together as chemical mediators that promote inflammation, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: L30 lists histamine, complement, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes. Lysozyme (L29) kills bacteria; it is not in the L30 list.

quiz.stem: Complement proteins circulate in plasma in an inactive form. Once activated, they:
options: Activate each other in a series, promoting inflammation, phagocytosis, and lysis
Become plasma cells that secrete antibody
Present antigen on MHC class II
quiz.explanation: L31: activation starts a series of reactions in which each complement protein activates the next; they promote inflammation, phagocytosis, and lyse bacteria.

quiz.stem: Which statement about complement is NOT on the slides?
options: It is produced by plasma cells
It is a group of over 20 plasma proteins
It can be activated by antibodies
quiz.explanation: L31 gives the other three. The slides never say plasma cells make complement; plasma cells produce antibodies (L44).

quiz.stem: A bacterium enters the blood. Parts of its wall bind complement proteins. Which outcome best explains how complement then destroys it directly?
quiz.explanation: L31: complement can directly lyse (rupture) bacterial cells.

quiz.stem: A virus infects a cell, which releases interferons. Which outcome is described on the slides?
options: Neighbouring noninfected cells produce antiviral proteins
quiz.explanation: L32: interferons bind noninfected cells and cause them to produce antiviral proteins; the infected cells cannot be protected.

quiz.stem: Some interferons can activate:
quiz.explanation: L32: some interferons can activate macrophages and natural killer cells.

quiz.stem: White blood cells leave the blood and move toward chemicals released by damaged tissue. This movement is called:
quiz.explanation: L33: movement toward these chemicals is called chemotaxis.

quiz.stem: According to the slides, white blood cells are produced in:
options: Red bone marrow and lymphatic tissues
quiz.explanation: L33: WBCs are produced in red bone marrow and lymphatic tissues.

quiz.stem: A patient has a skin infection with a collection of pus. Pus is mainly an accumulation of fluid, other cells, and dead:
quiz.explanation: L34: pus is an accumulation of fluid, dead neutrophils, and other cells at the site of an infection.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches the phagocyte with its feature?
options: Neutrophil: ingests more; macrophage: dies quickly
Neutrophil: forms the mononuclear phagocytic system; macrophage: dies quickly
Neutrophil: first to respond, dies quickly; macrophage: derived from monocytes, ingests more
Neutrophil: derived from monocytes; macrophage: first to respond
quiz.explanation: L34: neutrophils are first to respond but die quickly. L35: macrophages were monocytes and can ingest more than neutrophils.

quiz.stem: Monocytes and macrophages together form the:
quiz.explanation: L35: monocytes and macrophages form the mononuclear phagocytic system.

quiz.stem: Kupffer cells, dust cells, and microglia are all tissue-specific names for:
quiz.explanation: L35: macrophages are given specific names: Kupffer cells in liver, dust cells in lungs, microglia in CNS.

quiz.stem: Which cell is described as nonmotile and located in connective tissue?
quiz.explanation: L36: mast cells are nonmotile cells in connective tissue; basophils leave the blood and enter infected tissues.

quiz.stem: A patient with asthma has an increase in a white blood cell whose chemicals reduce inflammation associated with allergies and asthma. Which cell?
quiz.explanation: L36: eosinophils release chemicals to reduce inflammation associated with allergies and asthma.

quiz.stem: Basophils and mast cells produce the inflammatory response by releasing:
quiz.explanation: L36: they release histamine and leukotrienes to produce the inflammatory response.

quiz.stem: Natural killer cells differ from cytotoxic T cells on the slides because NK cells:
options: Recognize general classes of cells such as tumor or virus-infected cells
Are part of adaptive immunity and have memory
Require MHC class II to be activated
quiz.explanation: L37: NK cells recognize general classes of cells. Cytotoxic T cells bind a specific MHC class I/antigen complex (L75).

quiz.stem: Some interferons activate a lymphocyte that lyses virus-infected and tumor cells. That cell is the:
quiz.explanation: L32: some interferons activate NK cells. L37: NK cells recognize tumor or virus-infected cells and lyse them.

quiz.stem: In the inflammatory response, increased vascular permeability allows which substances to enter the tissue from the blood?
quiz.explanation: L38: increased vascular permeability allows fibrinogen and complement to enter the tissue from the blood.

quiz.stem: A splinter lets bacteria into the skin. Put the first events of Fig 14.9 in order: (1) bacteria contained and phagocytized, (2) chemical mediators released, (3) chemotaxis and increased permeability, (4) more WBCs at the site.
quiz.explanation: L39 (Fig 14.9): tissue damage → chemical mediators released → chemotaxis, permeability, blood flow → more WBCs and mediators → bacteria contained, destroyed, phagocytized.

quiz.stem: Why does the area around an infection become red during inflammation?
options: Vasodilation increases blood flow to the area
quiz.explanation: L38: vasodilation increases blood flow. L40: redness, heat, and swelling are due to increased blood flow and vascular permeability.

quiz.stem: A patient with a severe infection develops fever and a very high neutrophil count, then low blood pressure from fluid loss. This pattern is best described as:
quiz.explanation: L41: systemic inflammation adds neutrophil release, fever from pyrogens, and possible shock from fluid loss.

quiz.stem: Pyrogens produce fever by acting on the:
quiz.explanation: L41: pyrogens affect the temperature-regulating mechanism in the hypothalamus.

quiz.stem: All of the following are symptoms of local inflammation, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: L40 lists redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function. Fever is a feature of systemic inflammation (L41).

quiz.stem: A kidney transplant recipient's immune system attacks the new kidney. The trigger is best classified as:
quiz.explanation: L43: foreign antigens come from outside the body; tissue and organ transplants may be rejected.

quiz.stem: A disease in which self-antigens stimulate destruction of healthy tissue is called:
quiz.explanation: L43: autoimmune diseases are when self-antigens stimulate unwanted destruction of healthy tissue.

quiz.stem: The ability to respond with increasing effectiveness to successive exposures to the same antigen is:
quiz.explanation: L42: memory is the ability to respond with increasing effectiveness to successive exposures.

quiz.stem: All of the following are given as examples of antigens, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: L42 examples: bacteria, virus, pollen, food, drugs. Antibodies are the proteins made in response to antigens (L44).

quiz.stem: Which cell promotes or inhibits BOTH antibody-mediated and cell-mediated immunity?
quiz.explanation: L44: helper T cells promote or inhibit activities of both antibody-mediated and cell-mediated immunity.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches the type of adaptive immunity with its main cells?
options: Antibody-mediated: T cells; cell-mediated: B cells
Antibody-mediated: NK cells; cell-mediated: plasma cells
Antibody-mediated: B cells and plasma cells; cell-mediated: T cells
quiz.explanation: L44: antibody-mediated immunity uses B cells that become plasma cells; cell-mediated immunity involves T cells.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches the lymphocyte with where it matures?
options: B cell: red bone marrow; T cell: thymus gland
B cell: thymus; T cell: red bone marrow
B cell: liver; T cell: spleen
B cell: spleen; T cell: lymph node
quiz.explanation: L46: B cells mature in red bone marrow. L47: T cells mature in the thymus gland.

quiz.stem: A child is born without a functioning thymus. Which cells would fail to mature?
quiz.explanation: L47: T cells mature in the thymus gland. B cells mature in red bone marrow (L46).

quiz.stem: Put the path of a T cell in order (Fig 14.10): (1) lymph node, (2) red bone marrow as a pre-T cell, (3) thymus, (4) mature T cell.
quiz.explanation: L48 (Fig 14.10): stem cell → pre-T cell in red bone marrow → circulation → thymus (pre-T → T cell) → circulation → lymph node.

quiz.stem: Hemopoietic stem cells are found in:
quiz.explanation: L45: hemopoietic stem cells live in red bone marrow.

quiz.stem: A virus replicating inside a liver cell produces viral proteins. These internal antigens are displayed on:
quiz.explanation: L51: class I MHC molecules are on most nucleated cells and display internal antigens.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches the MHC class with its cells and antigens?
options: Class I: antigen-presenting cells only, external antigens
Class II: most nucleated cells, internal antigens
Class II: antigen-presenting cells, external antigens
Class I: red blood cells only, external antigens
quiz.explanation: L51: class I on most nucleated cells (internal); class II on antigen-presenting cells (external).

quiz.stem: All of the following are named as antigen-presenting cells, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: L51: antigen-presenting cells include macrophages, B cells, and other defense cells. Plasma cells are not listed.

quiz.stem: Interleukin-1 released by macrophages stimulates:
quiz.explanation: L52: interleukin-1 released by macrophages stimulates helper T cells.

quiz.stem: Cytokines are best described as:
options: Proteins secreted by a cell that regulate neighboring cells
Lipids that carry fats in lymph
Antibodies on the surface of B cells
quiz.explanation: L52: cytokines are proteins secreted by a cell that regulates neighboring cells.

quiz.stem: The virus that causes AIDS binds to which molecule, and therefore infects which cells?
options: MHC class I; all nucleated cells
quiz.explanation: L55: CD4 is also bound by the virus that causes AIDS; AIDS infects helper T cells.

quiz.stem: Arrange the helper T cell steps: (1) IL-2 stimulates division, (2) macrophage displays antigen on MHC II, (3) costimulation with CD4 and interleukins, (4) TCR binds the displayed antigen.
quiz.explanation: L53: step 1 APC display on MHC II, step 2 TCR interaction, step 3 costimulation (interleukins + CD4), step 4 IL-2 activation and division.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches the T cell, its surface glycoprotein, and the MHC class it connects to?
options: Helper T: CD4, MHC I; cytotoxic T: CD8, MHC II
Helper T: CD8, MHC II; cytotoxic T: CD4, MHC I
Helper T: CD4, MHC II; cytotoxic T: CD8, MHC I
Helper T: CD8, MHC I; cytotoxic T: CD4, MHC II
quiz.explanation: L55: helper T cells have CD4 (binds MHC II); cytotoxic T cells have CD8 (MHC I).

quiz.stem: A person meets the same antigen a second time. Which cells formed in step 6 of helper T activation respond?
quiz.explanation: L53 step 6: some daughter cells become memory T cells, which become active in future encounters with the same antigen.

quiz.stem: In B-cell proliferation, daughter cells that do NOT become plasma cells:
options: Reduce in size and become memory B cells
quiz.explanation: L56 step 6: daughter cells that do not become plasma cells reduce in size and become memory B cells.

quiz.stem: Order the B-cell steps: (1) plasma cells produce antibodies, (2) helper T binds the MHC II/antigen complex, (3) B cell takes in antigen and presents it on MHC II, (4) B cell divides repeatedly.
quiz.explanation: L56: take in and present on MHC II (steps 1–2), helper T binds (3), division (4), plasma cells make antibodies (5).

quiz.stem: Which cell actually secretes antibodies?
quiz.explanation: L56 step 5 and L44: B cells become plasma cells, which produce antibodies.

quiz.stem: A bacterial toxin circulates in the blood. Which branch of adaptive immunity is described as effective against it?
quiz.explanation: L58: antibody-mediated immunity is effective against antigens in body fluids, including toxins.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches the immunity with its target?
options: Antibody-mediated: tumor cells only; cell-mediated: pollen only
Antibody-mediated: viruses outside cells; cell-mediated: viruses inside cells
Antibody-mediated: intracellular protozoa; cell-mediated: toxins in blood
quiz.explanation: L58: antibody-mediated → viruses outside cells, toxins. L73: cell-mediated → antigens in cells, intracellular bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa.

quiz.stem: Which part of an antibody binds the epitope of an antigen?
options: Site of binding to mast cells
quiz.explanation: L59: the variable region binds to epitopes of antigen using the antigen-binding site.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches the antibody region with a function?
options: Variable region: attaches to mast cells; constant region: binds epitopes
Constant region: activates complement; variable region: binds a specific antigen
Variable region: same in each class; constant region: differs in each antibody
Constant region: binds a specific antigen; variable region: activates complement
quiz.explanation: L59: variable region binds only a specific antigen; constant region is the same per class and can activate complement and attach antibody to a cell.

quiz.stem: All of the following are labelled on the antibody in Fig 14.13, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: L60 (Fig 14.13) labels antigen-binding sites, heavy and light chains, variable and constant regions, complement-binding site, and site of binding to macrophages, basophils, and mast cells. No MHC site.

quiz.stem: A newborn is protected by antibodies that crossed the placenta from the mother. These antibodies are:
quiz.explanation: L62: IgG can cross the placenta and provide protection to the fetus.

quiz.stem: A patient receives the wrong ABO blood type and has a transfusion reaction. Which antibody class is responsible?
quiz.explanation: L63: IgM is responsible for transfusion reactions in the ABO blood system.

quiz.stem: Which antibody is most abundant in serum?
quiz.explanation: L62: IgG 80 to 85% in serum; L63–L65 give the lower values for the others.

quiz.stem: A breastfed infant receives antibodies in colostrum and milk that protect body surfaces. These are:
quiz.explanation: L64: IgA is found in colostrum and milk to provide immune protection to the newborn.

quiz.stem: A person with hay fever has an antibody bound to mast cells that stimulates inflammation. Which class?
quiz.explanation: L65: IgE binds to mast cells and basophils and stimulates the inflammatory response.

quiz.stem: All of the following are true of IgM, EXCEPT:
options: It crosses the placenta to protect the fetus
It acts as a receptor on B cells
It is often the first antibody produced
quiz.explanation: L63 lists the other three. Crossing the placenta is IgG (L62).

quiz.stem: Which antibody has the lowest concentration in serum?
quiz.explanation: L65: IgE 0.002% in serum; IgD is 0.2% (L66).

quiz.stem: All of the following are effects of antibodies, EXCEPT:
options: Presenting antigen on MHC class I
quiz.explanation: L67 lists inactivate antigen, bind antigens together, activate complement cascades, initiate release of inflammatory chemicals, facilitate phagocytosis.

quiz.stem: Which antibody effect is classified as DIRECT in Fig 14.14?
quiz.explanation: L68: direct effects are (a) inactivating the antigen and (b) binding antigens together; c–e on L69 are indirect.

quiz.stem: A child gets sick during the first exposure to a virus. Why do symptoms appear?
options: Memory B cells respond too quickly
Plasma cells need 3 to 14 days to produce enough antibody
quiz.explanation: L70: in the primary response, plasma cells take 3 to 14 days to produce enough antibody; meanwhile the person develops disease symptoms.

quiz.stem: Which cells make the secondary response faster than the primary response?
quiz.explanation: L71: the secondary response involves memory cells; memory B cells quickly divide to form plasma cells.

quiz.stem: According to Fig 14.15, the response time of the primary and secondary responses is:
options: Primary 3–14 days; secondary hours to a few days
quiz.explanation: L72 (Fig 14.15): longer response time (3–14 days) vs shorter response time (hours to a few days).

quiz.stem: Which statement about the secondary response is correct?
options: It produces more antibodies and new memory cells
It occurs on the first exposure to an antigen
It does not involve plasma cells
It produces fewer plasma cells than the primary response
quiz.explanation: L71–L72: memory B cells form plasma cells, more antibodies are produced, and new memory cells form.

quiz.stem: After an infection is cleared, which T cell turns off the immune system response?
quiz.explanation: L74: regulatory T cells turn off immune system response when antigen is gone.

quiz.stem: Cell-mediated immunity is effective against all of the following, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: L73: intracellular bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa. Toxins in body fluids are an antibody-mediated target (L58).

quiz.stem: Which T cell destroys antigen on contact?
quiz.explanation: L74: cytotoxic T cells destroy antigen on contact.

quiz.stem: A cytotoxic T cell is activated when its T-cell receptor binds:
quiz.explanation: L75 step 2: the cytotoxic T cell is activated when the T-cell receptor binds with the MHC class I/antigen complex.

quiz.stem: A patient's transplanted kidney is attacked by cells that bind its foreign antigens and make the cells lyse. Which cells?
quiz.explanation: L77: tissue transplants have foreign antigens that stimulate cytotoxic T-cell activity; they bind and cause the cells to lyse.

quiz.stem: Helper T cells increase cytotoxic T-cell activation mainly by releasing:
quiz.explanation: L75 step 4: helper T cells provide costimulation by releasing cytokines such as interleukin-2.

quiz.stem: Which is NOT a main effect of cytotoxic T cells?
quiz.explanation: L77 gives cytokine release (attracts macrophages, activates more cytotoxic T cells) and killing on contact. Antibodies come from plasma cells (L44).

quiz.stem: A child receives a measles vaccine and makes antibodies. This is:
quiz.explanation: L80: injection of antigens using vaccines, which cause the production of antibodies, is artificially acquired active immunity.

quiz.stem: A snakebite victim is injected with antibodies produced in a horse. This is:
quiz.explanation: L80: injection of antibodies from another person or animal is passive and called antiserum.

quiz.stem: A teenager recovers from mononucleosis and is immune afterward. This is:
quiz.explanation: L79: natural exposure causes antibody production and the person gets sick; example mononucleosis.

quiz.stem: Antibodies passed to a baby across the placenta are an example of:
quiz.explanation: L79: transfer of antibodies from mother to child (breast milk or placenta) is naturally acquired passive immunity.

quiz.stem: Inhibiting the immune system is listed as immunotherapy for:
quiz.explanation: L82: inhibiting immune system such as treatment for an autoimmune disease.

quiz.stem: All of the following are listed as effects of aging on immunity, EXCEPT:
options: Large increase in new T-cell production
quiz.explanation: L83: new T-cell production is LOST due to loss of thymus function; the other three are listed.

quiz.stem: An 80-year-old makes fewer new T cells than a child. The slide's explanation is:
quiz.explanation: L83: with age, production of new T cells is lost due to loss of thymus function.

quiz.stem: Fig 14.19 lists which two treatments for systemic lupus erythematosus?
quiz.explanation: L84 (Fig 14.19): Treatments: anti-inflammatory drugs, antimalarial drugs.

quiz.stem: All of the following are accessory digestive organs in Fig 16.1, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: D4 (Fig 16.1): accessory organs are salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas. The stomach is a major digestive organ.

quiz.stem: According to the overview slide, small molecules produced by enzymes are:
options: Absorbed into the blood and transported all over the body
quiz.explanation: D3: enzymes break particles into small molecules, which are absorbed into the blood and transported all over the body.

quiz.stem: The addition of liquids, enzymes, and mucus to ingested food is called:
quiz.explanation: D6: secretion is the addition of liquids, enzymes, and mucus to the ingested food.

quiz.stem: Movement of food back and forth in the digestive tract to mix it with enzymes is:
quiz.explanation: D5: mixing is the movement of food back and forth to mix it with enzymes and facilitate absorption. Propulsion moves food from one end to the other.

quiz.stem: A patient has a blockage that stops molecules from leaving the digestive tract and entering the blood or lymph. Which function is lost?
quiz.explanation: D6: absorption is the movement of molecules out of the digestive tract and into the blood or lymphatic system.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches an associated organ with where it empties?
quiz.explanation: D10: salivary glands → oral cavity; liver with gallbladder → small intestine; pancreas → small intestine.

quiz.stem: Which sequence lists part of the digestive tract in the correct order?
options: Stomach → esophagus → small intestine → large intestine
quiz.explanation: D9: oral cavity, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestines, large intestines, anus.

quiz.stem: All of the following are part of the digestive tract itself, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: D9 lists the tract; D10 lists the liver as an associated organ with a duct leading into the tract.

quiz.stem: Which layer contains blood vessels, nerves, small glands, and an ANS nerve plexus?
quiz.explanation: D11: submucosa contains blood vessels, nerves, small glands, ANS nerve plexus.

quiz.stem: The esophagus is lined with stratified epithelium rather than columnar epithelium because it needs:
quiz.explanation: D11: oral cavity, pharynx, and esophagus are stratified epithelium for protection against abrasion; stomach and intestine are columnar for secretion and absorption.

quiz.stem: Which statement about the outermost tunic is correct?
options: It is the layer that secretes mucus
It contains the oblique muscle layer
It is called serosa where peritoneum is present and adventitia where it is not
quiz.explanation: D12: serosa/adventitia is the outermost layer; serosa if peritoneum present, adventitia if not.

quiz.stem: Order the tunics from the lumen outward:
quiz.explanation: D11–D12: mucosa (innermost), submucosa (above mucosa), muscularis (above submucosa), serosa/adventitia (outermost).

quiz.stem: Which membrane lines the wall of the abdominal cavity?
quiz.explanation: D14: parietal peritoneum lines the wall of the abdominal cavity; visceral peritoneum covers the organs.

quiz.stem: A patient has potentially life-threatening inflammation of the serous membrane that lines the abdominal wall and covers the abdominal organs. This condition is:
quiz.explanation: D14: peritonitis is potentially life-threatening inflammation of the peritoneum.

quiz.stem: The fold connecting the greater curvature of the stomach to the transverse colon is the:
quiz.explanation: D16: greater omentum connects the greater curvature of stomach to transverse colon and posterior body wall.

quiz.stem: All of the following are in the nonmesenteric (formerly retroperitoneal) domain, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: D15 lists duodenum, pancreas, ascending and descending colon, rectum, kidneys, adrenal glands, urinary bladder.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches the structure with its muscle or tissue?
options: Hard palate: skeletal muscle; soft palate: bone
Uvula: bone; hard palate: connective tissue
quiz.explanation: D18: lips formed by orbicularis oris; buccinator muscles within the cheeks. D24: hard palate bone; soft palate skeletal muscle and connective tissue.

quiz.stem: The posterior extension of the soft palate is the:
quiz.explanation: D24: uvula, posterior extension of the soft palate.

quiz.stem: A patient cannot keep food between the teeth because the muscle that flattens the cheeks against the teeth is paralyzed. Which muscle?
quiz.explanation: D18: within the cheeks are the buccinator muscles, which flatten the cheeks against the teeth.

quiz.stem: Which tissue forms the bulk of the tooth?
quiz.explanation: D20: the bulk of the tooth is formed by a cellular tissue called dentin.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly describes dentin and enamel?
options: Dentin is cellular; enamel is acellular and extremely hard
Enamel forms the bulk of the tooth; dentin covers the crown
Dentin is acellular; enamel is cellular
quiz.explanation: D20: dentin is a cellular tissue; enamel is extremely hard and acellular.

quiz.stem: A patient's teeth loosen as the gingiva, periodontal ligaments, and alveolar bone become inflamed and degenerate. This is:
quiz.explanation: D21: periodontal disease is inflammation and degeneration of the periodontal ligaments, gingiva, and alveolar bone.

quiz.stem: How many more teeth does a healthy adult have than a child with a full set of primary teeth?
quiz.explanation: D20: 32 adult teeth and 20 primary teeth; 32 − 20 = 12.

quiz.stem: Teeth are held in pockets of bone called:
quiz.explanation: D21: teeth are held in place within pockets in the bone called alveoli.

quiz.stem: A child has painful swelling in front of both ears from inflammation of a serous salivary gland. Which gland is affected?
quiz.explanation: D26: parotid, serous glands anterior to each ear; mumps is inflammation of the parotid glands.

quiz.stem: Which salivary gland produces primarily mucous secretions?
quiz.explanation: D26: sublingual glands produce primarily mucous.

quiz.stem: Which component of saliva provides lubrication?
quiz.explanation: D28: mucous portion contains mucin for lubrication.

quiz.stem: A student before an oral exam has a dry mouth because they are nervous. Which explains this?
options: Sympathetic stimulation shuts down saliva production
quiz.explanation: D31: sympathetic stimulation increases the mucous content of saliva and shuts down saliva production when frightened or nervous.

quiz.stem: All of the following are functions of saliva, EXCEPT:
options: Dissolving food particles so they can be tasted
quiz.explanation: D25 and D29 list the other three. Pepsin is a stomach enzyme (D43).

quiz.stem: According to Fig 16.8, which enzyme converts trypsinogen to trypsin?
quiz.explanation: D30 (Fig 16.8): Enterokinase. Converts trypsinogen to trypsin. Figure-only; not in slide text.

quiz.stem: The lower third of the esophagus is made of:
quiz.explanation: D34: upper third skeletal, middle third skeletal and smooth, lower third smooth muscle.

quiz.stem: Which part of the pharynx is NOT described as a passageway for food and drink?
quiz.explanation: D33: oropharynx and laryngopharynx are passageways for food/drink; the nasopharynx is listed without that role.

quiz.stem: Another name for the cardiac sphincter is the:
quiz.explanation: D34: joins stomach at cardiac sphincter (lower esophageal sphincter).

quiz.stem: During which phase of swallowing does the epiglottis cover the larynx?
quiz.explanation: D35: pharyngeal phase, swallowing reflex initiated when bolus stimulates receptors in oropharynx; epiglottis covers the larynx.

quiz.stem: Order the phases of swallowing:
quiz.explanation: D35: voluntary (bolus pushed into oropharynx), pharyngeal (reflex), esophageal (pharynx to stomach).

quiz.stem: A patient chokes because food enters the larynx. Failure of which event is most directly responsible?
quiz.explanation: D35: in the pharyngeal phase, the epiglottis covers the larynx.

quiz.stem: Which region of the stomach is to the left of, and superior to, the cardiac part?
quiz.explanation: D39: the fundus is to the left of, and superior to, the cardiac part.

quiz.stem: After a large meal the stomach expands. Which structures allow it to stretch?
quiz.explanation: D40: rugae are large folds that allow stomach to stretch.

quiz.stem: The stomach differs from the rest of the tract because its muscularis adds:
options: A second circular layer outside the serosa
quiz.explanation: D12 and D40: the stomach adds an oblique layer (outer longitudinal, middle circular, inner oblique).

quiz.stem: All of the following are produced by the stomach, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: D38: stomach produces mucus, hydrochloric acid, protein-digesting enzymes. Bile is from the liver (D74).

quiz.stem: A patient lacks intrinsic factor and cannot absorb vitamin B12 well. Which stomach cells are most likely damaged?
quiz.explanation: D42: parietal cells produce hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. D44: intrinsic factor binds vitamin B12.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches the stomach cell with its product?
quiz.explanation: D42: chief cells produce pepsinogen; parietal cells produce HCl and intrinsic factor; mucous neck cells produce mucus.

quiz.stem: All of the following stomach cells are found in the gastric glands, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: D42: surface mucous cells produce mucus that coats and protects the stomach (not in gastric glands).

quiz.stem: The stomach's pH of about 2.0 is produced by:
quiz.explanation: D43: hydrochloric acid produces a pH of about 2.0 in the stomach.

quiz.stem: A patient with heartburn takes a drug that blocks the pump parietal cells need to make acid. This drug is a:
quiz.explanation: D45: proton pump inhibitors block the proton pump in parietal cells needed to make acid.

quiz.stem: A patient's parietal cells stop making intrinsic factor. Which explains a later fall in red blood cell production?
options: Less pepsin is converted to pepsinogen
Less vitamin B12 is absorbed by the small intestine
More amylase is secreted by the pancreas
More bile is produced by the liver
quiz.explanation: D44: intrinsic factor binds vitamin B12, making it more readily absorbed; B12 is important in red blood cell production.

quiz.stem: Which statement about pepsin is correct?
options: It is formed when acid activates pepsinogen
It is made by the pancreas
It is secreted active by parietal cells
quiz.explanation: D43: acid activates pepsinogen to pepsin; D42: chief cells produce pepsinogen.

quiz.stem: Antacids relieve heartburn by:
quiz.explanation: D45: antacids neutralize acids in the stomach.

quiz.stem: A hungry student smells food and the stomach begins secreting acid before eating. Which phase is this?
quiz.explanation: D47: cephalic phase, stomach secretions are initiated by sight, smell, taste, or food thought.

quiz.stem: Which is the most potent stimulator of hydrochloric acid secretion?
quiz.explanation: D47: histamine is the most potent stimulator of hydrochloric acid secretion.

quiz.stem: During the gastric phase, gastrin secretion is stimulated by:
options: Peptides produced by pepsin acting on proteins
quiz.explanation: D49 step 4: peptides, produced by the action of pepsin on proteins, stimulate the secretion of gastrin.

quiz.stem: Very acidic chyme (pH 1.8) enters the duodenum. What happens to gastric secretion and why?
options: It is unchanged; the duodenum has no receptors
It increases; histamine is released from the duodenum
It decreases; secretin is released and local reflexes inhibit secretion
quiz.explanation: D51: acidic chyme (pH < 2.0) inhibits CNS stimulation, initiates inhibitory local reflexes, and secretin released in response to low pH inhibits gastric secretions.

quiz.stem: Which statement about the intestinal phase is correct?
options: It is started by stomach distention
It is started by the thought of food
quiz.explanation: D51: the intestinal phase is controlled by acidic chyme entering the duodenum and decreases gastric secretions (Fig 16.12c: secretions inhibited).

quiz.stem: Order the cephalic phase: (1) gastrin and histamine stimulate more secretion, (2) sight or smell of food, (3) medulla sends impulses along the vagus nerves, (4) enteric neurons stimulate HCl, pepsin, mucus, and intrinsic factor.
quiz.explanation: D47 steps 1–4: stimulus → medulla and vagus → postganglionic neurons stimulate secretion → gastrin and histamine add more secretion.

quiz.stem: A patient eats a high-fat meal. About how long will the stomach take to empty?
quiz.explanation: D53: stomach empties every 4 hours after a regular meal, and 6 to 8 hours after a high-fat meal.

quiz.stem: Which contractions force chyme through the pyloric sphincter?
quiz.explanation: D53: peristaltic waves are stronger contractions that force chyme toward and through the pyloric sphincter.

quiz.stem: Which part of the small intestine contains the bile and pancreatic ducts?
quiz.explanation: D56: duodenum contains bile and pancreatic ducts.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches the segment with its description?
options: Jejunum: second part, primary site of nutrient absorption
Jejunum: third part, contains bile ducts
quiz.explanation: D56–D57: duodenum first (25 cm); jejunum second (2.5 m, primary absorption); ileum third (3.5 m).

quiz.stem: Which is the longest part of the small intestine?
quiz.explanation: D57: jejunum 2.5 meters; ileum 3.5 meters. D56: duodenum 25 cm.

quiz.stem: The lymphatic capillary in the core of each villus is the:
quiz.explanation: D59: each villus has a loose connective tissue core containing blood capillaries and a lymphatic capillary called a lacteal.

quiz.stem: Which small-intestine cell may help protect the epithelium from bacteria?
quiz.explanation: D60: granular cells may help protect the intestinal epithelium from bacteria.

quiz.stem: Lymphatic nodules that are numerous in the ileum are called:
quiz.explanation: D61: lymphatic nodules called Peyer's patches are numerous in the ileum.

quiz.stem: A disease flattens the villi and microvilli of the small intestine. Which outcome best follows from the slides?
options: More Peyer's patches in the duodenum
quiz.explanation: D59: circular folds, villi, and microvilli are modifications to increase surface area; D55: the small intestine is the major absorptive organ.

quiz.stem: Mucous glands located in the SUBMUCOSA of the duodenum are the:
quiz.explanation: D61: the submucosa of the duodenum contains mucous glands called duodenal glands. Crypts of Lieberkühn are tubular glands of the mucosa.

quiz.stem: Which contractions of the small intestine mix contents over short distances?
quiz.explanation: D64: segmental contractions are propagated for only short distances and mix intestinal contents.

quiz.stem: What prevents material in the large intestine from moving back into the ileum?
quiz.explanation: D65: the ileocecal valve prevents movement from the large intestine back into the ileum.

quiz.stem: Brush-border disaccharidases convert:
quiz.explanation: D63: disaccharidases enzymatically break down disaccharides into monosaccharides.

quiz.stem: Nutrient-rich blood from the digestive organs reaches the liver through the:
quiz.explanation: D69: hepatic portal vein delivers nutrient-rich blood from the digestive organs.

quiz.stem: All of the following are found in a portal triad, EXCEPT:
options: Branch of the hepatic portal vein
quiz.explanation: D70: portal triad contains branches of hepatic artery, hepatic portal vein, hepatic duct. The central vein is in the center of the lobule (D69).

quiz.stem: Order the flow of blood through the liver: (1) hepatic veins, (2) central vein, (3) hepatic sinusoids, (4) inferior vena cava.
quiz.explanation: D69–D71: sinusoids between cords drain to the central vein; central veins unite to form hepatic veins, which empty into the inferior vena cava.

quiz.stem: Which liver structure contains phagocytic cells that remove foreign particles from the blood?
quiz.explanation: D71: hepatic sinusoids contain phagocytic cells that remove foreign particles from blood. (L35 names the liver's macrophages Kupffer cells.)

quiz.stem: The common bile duct is formed by the union of the:
options: Pancreatic duct and accessory pancreatic duct
Common hepatic duct and cystic duct
quiz.explanation: D72: common bile duct formed from common hepatic duct and cystic duct.

quiz.stem: A gallstone blocks the common bile duct just before the duodenal papilla. Bile from which source can no longer reach the duodenum?
options: Neither; bile enters through the cystic duct
Both the liver and the gallbladder
quiz.explanation: D72: the cystic duct (gallbladder) and common hepatic duct (liver) join to form the common bile duct, which joins the pancreatic duct at the duodenal papilla.

quiz.stem: Order the bile ducts from the liver outward:
options: Common bile duct → common hepatic duct → hepatic ducts
Hepatic ducts → common hepatic duct → common bile duct
Cystic duct → hepatic ducts → common hepatic duct
Hepatic ducts → cystic duct → pancreatic duct
quiz.explanation: D72: hepatic ducts (left and right) form the common hepatic duct, which with the cystic duct forms the common bile duct.

quiz.stem: A patient with liver failure has high blood ammonia. Which liver function has failed?
quiz.explanation: D75: the liver removes ammonia from the blood and converts it to urea that is eliminated in the urine.

quiz.stem: A patient with severe liver disease bleeds easily. Which slide-listed function best explains this?
options: Synthesis of clotting factors and fibrinogen
quiz.explanation: D75: the liver can synthesize blood proteins such as albumin, fibrinogen, globulins, and clotting factors.

quiz.stem: All of the following are stored by the liver, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: D74: the liver stores glycogen, fat, vitamins, copper, and iron.

quiz.stem: Bile pigments excreted in bile come from the breakdown of:
quiz.explanation: D74: bile contains bile pigments that result from hemoglobin breakdown.

quiz.stem: Which hormone, carried in blood from the duodenum, makes the gallbladder contract and its sphincters relax?
quiz.explanation: D76 step 3: cholecystokinin stimulates the gallbladder to contract and the sphincters to relax.

quiz.stem: Where are most bile salts reabsorbed?
quiz.explanation: D76 step 4: over 90% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum.

quiz.stem: A patient has the ileum surgically removed. Which outcome do the slides best predict?
options: More bile salts lost in the feces
quiz.explanation: D76: over 90% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum; this recycling reduces the loss of bile salts in the feces.

quiz.stem: Bile salts stimulate further bile secretion. This is an example of:
quiz.explanation: D76 step 4: bile salts increase bile secretion through a positive-feedback system.

quiz.stem: Which pancreatic enzyme digests lipids?
quiz.explanation: D81: the pancreatic enzyme lipase is a lipid-digesting enzyme.

quiz.stem: All of the following are pancreatic protein-digesting enzymes, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: D80: trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase. Pepsin is secreted by the stomach (D101).

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches pancreatic tissue with its product?
options: Islets: insulin and glucagon; acini: digestive enzymes
quiz.explanation: D78: endocrine tissues have pancreatic islets that produce insulin and glucagon; exocrine acini produce digestive enzymes.

quiz.stem: A patient's pancreatic duct is blocked. Which digestive problem is most directly expected in the duodenum?
options: Acidic chyme is not neutralized and enzymes cannot work well
quiz.explanation: D78: acini enzymes travel through ducts to the duodenum. D80: bicarbonate ions neutralize acidic chyme so the digestive enzymes can function.

quiz.stem: Very acidic chyme enters the duodenum. Which pancreatic response follows?
options: Secretin release → watery secretion rich in bicarbonate
quiz.explanation: D82 step 2: acidic chyme stimulates secretin release; secretin stimulates a watery secretion rich in HCO3−.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches the hormone with the pancreatic secretion it stimulates?
quiz.explanation: D82: secretin → watery secretion rich in HCO3−; cholecystokinin → enzyme-rich solution.

quiz.stem: A fatty meal reaches the duodenum. Which hormone increases both gallbladder contraction and enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion?
quiz.explanation: D82: fatty acids and amino acids stimulate cholecystokinin release, which stimulates an enzyme-rich pancreatic solution. D76: cholecystokinin also makes the gallbladder contract.

quiz.stem: Which anal sphincter is skeletal muscle under conscious control?
quiz.explanation: D86: external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle and under conscious control; the internal is smooth muscle, unconscious.

quiz.stem: Bands of longitudinal muscle on the colon are called:
quiz.explanation: D85: longitudinal muscle forms bands called teniae coli.

quiz.stem: A patient on long-term antibiotics that kill gut microbes is at risk of low levels of which vitamin, according to the slides?
quiz.explanation: D86: microbes synthesize vitamin K.

quiz.stem: Order the large intestine from proximal to distal:
options: Ascending → cecum → transverse → descending → rectum → sigmoid
Cecum → transverse → ascending → sigmoid → descending → rectum
Rectum → sigmoid → descending → transverse → ascending → cecum
Cecum → ascending colon → transverse colon → descending colon → sigmoid colon → rectum
quiz.explanation: D84–D85: cecum joins small intestine; colon = ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid; rectum begins at sigmoid colon and ends at anal canal.

quiz.stem: Distention of the rectal wall by feces stimulates:
quiz.explanation: D88: movement of feces into the rectum distends the rectal wall and stimulates the defecation reflex.

quiz.stem: According to the digestive-process slide, most absorption occurs in the:
quiz.explanation: D89: most absorption occurs in the duodenum and jejunum, although some occurs in the stomach and ileum.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches the nutrient with its digestion end product (Fig 16.23)?
quiz.explanation: D90 (Fig 16.23): carbohydrates → monosaccharides; lipids → fatty acids and monoglycerides; proteins → amino acids.

quiz.stem: Chewing food into smaller pieces is an example of:
quiz.explanation: D89: mechanical digestion is breaking food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion is enzymatic breakdown.

quiz.stem: Glucose enters intestinal epithelial cells by:
quiz.explanation: D93 step 1: glucose is absorbed by cotransport with Na+ into intestinal epithelial cells.

quiz.stem: A drug blocks the Na+–K+ pump of intestinal epithelial cells. Which step of glucose absorption fails first?
options: Facilitated diffusion into the capillary only
Cotransport, because the sodium gradient is lost
quiz.explanation: D93 step 2: cotransport is driven by a sodium gradient established by a Na+–K+ pump.

quiz.stem: Order the glucose steps: (1) facilitated diffusion out of the cell, (2) cotransport with Na+ into the cell, (3) hepatic portal vein to the liver, (4) entry into villus capillaries.
quiz.explanation: D93 steps 1–4: cotransport in; (gradient by pump); facilitated diffusion out; capillaries of villi → hepatic portal vein → liver.

quiz.stem: Absorbed glucose travels to the liver through which vessel?
quiz.explanation: D93 step 4: glucose enters capillaries of the villi and is carried through the hepatic portal vein to the liver.

quiz.stem: Fatty acids and monoglycerides enter intestinal epithelial cells by:
options: Active transport by the Na+–K+ pump
quiz.explanation: D95: fatty acids and monoglycerides pass by simple diffusion into the intestinal epithelial cells.

quiz.stem: Unlike glucose and amino acids, chylomicrons leave the intestine by entering:
quiz.explanation: D97: chylomicrons enter the lacteals and are carried through the lymphatic system to the blood. D93 and D104: glucose and amino acids enter capillaries and the hepatic portal vein.

quiz.stem: Bile salts cannot reach a patient's duodenum. Which step of fat digestion is most directly affected?
options: Absorption of water in the colon
quiz.explanation: D95: bile salts surround fatty acids and monoglycerides to form micelles.

quiz.stem: Order lipid absorption: (1) chylomicrons enter lacteals, (2) micelles form, (3) triglycerides re-form inside the cell, (4) protein coat added and exocytosis.
quiz.explanation: D95: micelle formation; D97: conversion to triglycerides, protein coat → chylomicrons, exocytosis, lacteals.

quiz.stem: Lipoproteins are needed for lipid transport because:
options: Lipids are too large to cross capillaries
Lipids are digested only in the liver
Lipids must be converted to glucose first
Lipids are not water soluble, while lymph and blood are watery
quiz.explanation: D99: since lymph and blood contain water and lipids are not water soluble, lipoproteins are necessary for transport.

quiz.stem: Trypsin, chymotrypsin, and carboxypeptidase are secreted by the pancreas:
options: In an inactive state, then activated in the small intestine
In an active state into the stomach
In an inactive state, then activated by bile in the liver
quiz.explanation: D101: the pancreas secretes them into the small intestine in an inactive state; in the small intestine these enzymes are activated.

quiz.stem: Absorbed amino acids reach the liver through:
options: Villus capillaries and the hepatic portal vein
quiz.explanation: D104 step 4: amino acids enter blood capillaries in the villi and are carried by the hepatic portal vein to the liver.

quiz.stem: Which statement about amino acid absorption is correct?
options: All amino acids enter by simple diffusion in micelles
Amino acids are packaged into chylomicrons
Many, but not all, amino acids are absorbed by cotransport with a Na+ gradient
quiz.explanation: D104 step 2: many, but not all, amino acids are absorbed by cotransport with a Na+ gradient, similar to glucose.

quiz.stem: Which enzyme is NOT secreted by the pancreas?
quiz.explanation: D101: pepsin is secreted by the stomach; the pancreas secretes trypsin, chymotrypsin, and carboxypeptidase.

quiz.stem: How are minerals absorbed across the small intestine wall?
quiz.explanation: D106: minerals are actively transported across wall of small intestine.

quiz.stem: According to Fig 16.29, where is most of the fluid in the digestive tract absorbed?
quiz.explanation: D107 (Fig 16.29): 92% absorbed in small intestine; 6–7% in large intestine; 1% in feces.

quiz.stem: If 99% of the water entering the intestine is absorbed, what percentage is NOT absorbed?
quiz.explanation: D106: 99% of water entering intestine is absorbed, so 100 − 99 = 1% is not (Fig 16.29 also shows 1% in feces).

quiz.stem: All of the following are effects of aging on the digestive system, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: D108: mucus and digestive enzyme secretions DECREASE; motility and blood supply decrease; GERD increases.

quiz.stem: Fig 16.30 lists which treatment for diarrhea?
quiz.explanation: D109 (Fig 16.30): Treatments: replacing lost fluid and ions; eating a bland diet without dairy.

flags.text: 3.2's slide L20 says the thymus "produces and matures T lymphocytes"; L45-L47 say pre-T cells come from red bone marrow and T cells only MATURE in the thymus. This site uses L45-L47. No question depends on where T cells are "produced".

Serum percentages on L62-L66 (IgG 80-85, IgM 5-10, IgA 15, IgD 0.2, IgE 0.002) add up to more than 100% at the upper ends. Single values and the ranking (IgG most, IgE least) are quizzed; sums are not.

L74: helper T cells "help form B cells and promote production of T_C" (T_C is an image on the slide). "Help form B cells" is not explained on any slide, so it is quoted, not interpreted, and not quizzed.
L53 and L56 say "(described in more detail below)", "(described below)", "(only four are shown in this figure)". This is textbook wording; the "below" text is not on any slide.
The secondary response time "hours to a few days" is only in Fig 14.15 (L72), not in the slide text.
L35 names the liver's macrophages "Kupffer cells". D71 and Fig 16.17 only say "phagocytic cells" in the hepatic sinusoids. The link is stated only as: L35 names them, D71 places them.

D45 says heartburn is "also called gastritis". [Inference] Those terms are not normally used as synonyms, but no outside source is used here. The slide wording is shown as is, and no question depends on the two being the same. Ask the professor if it matters.
D55: small intestine "6 meters". D56-D57: duodenum 25 cm + jejunum 2.5 m + ileum 3.5 m = 6.25 m. Single lengths are quizzed; the sum is not.

D63 and Fig 16.24: peptidases break proteins/peptides into AMINO ACIDS. D103: peptidases "further break down small peptides into tripeptides". This site uses D63's wording; the D103 statement is not quizzed.
D91: salivary and pancreatic amylases split polysaccharides into disaccharides. Fig 16.24 (D92) oral-cavity box: complex carbohydrates -> "polysaccharides and disaccharides". Questions use D91.

Fig 16.8 (D30) and Fig 16.2 (D7) contain items that are not in any slide text: lingual and gastric lipase, cholesterol esterase, ribonuclease, deoxyribonuclease, enterokinase, sucrase, maltase, isomaltase, lactase, stomach absorption of water/alcohol/aspirin. They are Tier 3 only.
Lipoprotein composition percentages exist only in Fig 16.27 (D100). Tier 3 only.
The slides go "Oral Cavity 1" (D18) -> "Oral Cavity 3" (D19). There is no "Oral Cavity 2" slide in the PDF. [Unverified] whether a slide was removed.

D72: "Cystic duct: joins common hepatic duct that drains gallbladder" is ambiguous about which duct drains the gallbladder. Fig 16.18 (D73) shows the cystic duct coming from the gallbladder; the site uses that reading.

"compliment" (L62, L63) read as complement; title "Immunoglobins" as immunoglobulins; L67 "Active complement cascades" as activate; L37 "produce in" as produced in; L44 "Two Type" as two types; L71 "quickly divided" as divide.

D31 "shits down saliva production" read as shuts down; D29 "needed to unimpaired speech" and "dissolved chemicals" as needed for unimpaired speech / dissolve; D35 "larnyx" as larynx; D38 "acidic ph" as pH; D45 "an increased in" as an increase in; D76 "bi salts" as bile salts; D98 figure "Cylomicron" as chylomicron; D61 "Peyers Patches" as Peyer's patches.
